speechtext: The House again in committee on Bill No. 83 respecting banks and banking, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, I asked last night that this clause might be allowed to stand over as it was my intention to submit an amendment. I have decided, however, not to bring that amendment forward as I am of the opinion that it would not receive the support of the committee. I would like to say a few words in regard to this section.
I think it is a mistake for this committee to say that people should not be allowed to start a bank in this country unless and until the new organization has a subscribed capital of S500,000. I would urge upon the minister the desirability of making it somewhat easier for any group of individuals in this country to get together and start a bank if they so desire. At the present time the banking business in this country is in the hands of a very small group of individuals, and I do not see that there is any possibility of relief from the present situation unless the act is amended to allow banks to start with a smaller capitalization. The reason I am not moving an amendment is that I do not know just what figure to suggest that might meet with the approval of this committee, but I do want to point out that by this legislation we are making it impossible for the people in
Bank Act

any town or village to start a bank even if they desire to do so and have money sufficient for the purpose. I do not think it is right for this parliament to say that these people should not be allowed to start a bank. Surely, that is carrying the prohibition too far. I would respectfully urge upon the Minister of Finance to take this matter into his most serious consideration and see whether it would not be wise to allow the banks to be started with a smaller subscribed capital than is here provided. The banking system in the United States has been built up through the formation of very small banks in the main. There are many banks in the United States which started with a capital of $25,000 and which have now a paid up capital of $1,000,000 or more, and it does seem to me that it would be possible for us to build up some banks in Canada under that same system, particularly as we now have upon the statute books the War Finance Act which allows banks to re-discount their securities with the Finance Department. Without discussing the matter at any greater length I would earnestly urge this upon the Minister of Finance for his consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The question referred to by my hon. friend is undoubtedly one of much interest and importance. It has been well considered by the department, and I think I may say it was pretty carefully considered by the committee. There is certainly something to be said in favour of the hon. member's suggestion. On the other hand, there aie several reasons which I think can be properly urged against it. To begin with, in these days of big things a small enterprise in any line of business will have trouble in competing with the larger concern. A small bank will have a great difficulty in competing with a larger institution. There are certain expenses incidental to management which have to apply to a small bank and also to a large one, and it is only because these expenses can be distributed over a large area in the case of the larger institution that the cost of the organization and management may be deemed reasonable. That in itself is the reason why, I think, a small bank would have, from the very beginning, great difficulty in holding its own.
Then there is another consideration. The argument for a small bank is that it appeals to the local feeling, appeals to the local pride. There is certainly force in that. But that which is an argument at one moment in its favour is really a good argument against it. The tendency of the small bank, appealing to tMr. Coote.l
local feeling, appealing to local pride, is to become so identified with local affairs that it, so to speak, puts all its eggs into one basket, and when trouble occurs the small bank, dependent upon local business, has an exceedingly difficult task to exist. I think, take it all in all, that any bank which is organized in Canada at a smaller capital than that which i3 required under the existing law would have a poor chance of success. I doubt whether any honourable member who thinks it out would do well to advise anybody to put money into a small bank in Canada with the expectation that it could compete successfully against the larger institutions.

The minister has said that the danger in connection with the small local banks is that they are apt to become localized in their activities and, having put all their eggs in one basket, to use the illustration he mentioned, would have greater difficulty in existing when trouble came. Does he not think that a rediscounting system in connection with the local bank would overcome the danger which he anticipates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That raises another
question. I think the activities of the small bank would be localized. Even though it might utilize a system of rediscounting in the way suggested to my hon. friend it would still be a local institution. The danger is that it would become so local and so interested in a few local enterprises that, I think the experience has shown in Canada- I do not want to discuss the American system-the small bank would be a menace to the financial situation, and would not tend to promote that stability in financial affairs which, I am sure, hon. gentlemen opposite are as anxious to maintain as I am.

I would like to question the
argument of the Minister of Finance when he refers to the alleged difficulty the small banks might have in competing wtih the larger banks. As a matter of fact in the United States they have developed a vast number of smaller banks. These banks, it is true, have failed in a number of cases, but I think the statistics given in the committee on Banking and Commerce showed that the proportion of failures was considerably less than in Canada. Now, these are facts, and while everyone would admit the existence of certain difficulties the small banks would have to face, those who look at the matter fairly must also admit that there are certain very distinct advantages, not only from the standpoint of utility to the neighbourhood, to the community, but from the standpoint of

Bank Act
actual efficiency and operation-for example the low overhead expenses. We ought, I think, as a matter of principle, to allow free competition between the large branch bank systems such as we have in Canada and the local bank system. Nobody knows which is the best? How can you tell if you do not try? If the legislation practically prohibits the formation of any small banks the argument surely is not valid that the small bank cannot compete against its larger competitor and is of no use. I submit that in the United States, a country very like our own, the small bank has proven entirely satisfactory, particularly since it has been linked up with the federal reserve system of that country. I feel that this is a matter which must receive consideration sooner or later, and we might as well face the situation now. The experience in Canada has been referred to by the Minister of Finance. I presume he refers to a number of failures of small banks years ago; but we have had a number of failures of larger banks, and I do not know that any evidence has been submitted in the standing committee or in the Committee of the Whole which would show that the proportion of failures in small banks has been any greater in volume than the proportion in our larger banks. I quite agree with the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) that there is not much prospect of getting anything like this system in operation, particularly as it was turned down in the Banking and Commerce committee. However, I would like to place myself on record as stating that in my opinion we ought to allow a fair field and no favours and not prohibit the smaller bank, which has been very useful elsewhere, from getting a start in Canada. I think it may be particularly useful and particularly stable when we link it up with the federal reserve system, or with the Treasury Board under our Finance Act.

I believe that the capitalization of the banks at the present time is entirely too large. The Minister of Finance has referred to the disadvantage of localizing banks. In the Maritime provinces we are suffering from the disadvantages of centralization. Twenty years ago, Mr. Chairman, we had, if I remember rightly, fourteen banks with their head offices in those provinces. We had fourteen boards of directors, comprising the leading and best business minds of the Maritime provinces, sitting around the boards of those respective banks and considering the needs and necessities of the Maritime provinces to a large extent. They knew our difficulties, they sympathized with our ambitions,
and we were able at that time to secure banking accommodation in a rather liberal way. Now, Mr. Chairman, we have not a single bank with bank directors sitting round the board in the Maritime provinces; and it has been said by someone, and I guess it is probably true, that there is no individual, and no board of directors in these provinces having the real right to-day to advance even $20,000 on a credit without the matter being referred to the head office in Montreal or Toronto. Now, I am not attacking the bank directors in Montreal and Toronto, nor am I attacking the banking system as it exists today. I think, taking it all in all, that it was, in its inception at any rate, a very great banking system. But there may be, and I think there is necessity to-day for some amendments. Nevertheless, the fact is, Mr. Chairman, that the man in the Maritime provinces in order to get credit must first go to a local bank manager. This manager may not understand very many of our difficulties, but the system is to report to the head office, and the board of directors in the head office will issue or deny that credit, depending largely upon the recommendation of the local manager. The local manager may so report as to cause the application to be received with considerable favour. He may be a local banker in whom the head office has very great confidence, and his recommendation may receive more consideration than that of some other bank manager.

Has not the Bank of Nova
Scotia its head office in Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Nominally.

Nominally it has its head
office in the city of Halifax where you would think the head office of the Bank of Nova Scotia should be; but practically the head office of that bank is one thousand miles away from the province from which it derives its name.
How does my hon. friend explain the disappearance of thes-e small banks and the location of the headquarters elsewhere?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not a small bank,
it is a large bank.
It is a large bank, yes. Moreover, how would my hon. friend prevent the same thing occurring to the small banks of which he advocates the creation?

I presume the reason for the change of head office to Montreal and Toronto lies in the tendency in Canada towards centralization along all lines. I am not asking that
40S0
Bank Act

legislation be passed here to compel the formation of banks in the Maritime provinces; but what I do say is that we should not shut the door against the formation of new banks, even though we may lose later on. I know of individual cases of clients of mine who have suffered very serious injury through a lack of knowledge on the part of the local bank manager, on one hand, and, on the other, a lack of knowledge on the part of the directors sitting a thousand miles away considering the case. It is natural that men in Nova Scotia or in the Maritime provinces should know more about that part of the country, the men, the character of borrowers, than any body of men can possibly know sitting a thousand miles away. I was not a member of the committee on Banking and Commerce; in fact, I was not here during the greater part of the session. But I have taken the trouble to read the minutes of the proceedings of that committee, and I find that a motion was made there to reduce the amount to $50,000. I would vote against that, because I think the amount is too small. On the other hand, however, I certainly think that $500,000 is too large a sum to fix as the minimum in this day; we might very well reduce it to $150,000 or $250,000 in order that it might be easier for men in the outlying parts of the Dominion to form banks to deal with local affairs. People ask, what is the matter with the Maritime provinces, and why is it that we are losing our population? Well, there are several reasons, one being of course the high cost of transportation. But among the several reasons that may be offered for this condition, one of the most outstanding is the fact that we have lost our money control in the Maritime provinces, so that it is exceedingly difficult to secure for local enterprises sufficient capital to carry on when we have to appeal to a board a thousand miles away who very often know us not.

If the question of small local banks were possible and practical I would very heartily endorse it; I fancy that nobody, in principle, is opposed to smaller local banks operating within a limited area. Indeed, the present Canadian act is not against small banks because it expressly provides that a bank with a capitalization of $500,000 may start business. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) deprecates the fact that in the Maritime provinces we have no small banks. I might say to him, however, that in the city of Halifax as well as in St. John, there would not be the slightest difficulty whatever in securing $500,000 of capital with which to start a bank and operate it locally if the people thought that it could exist and successfully continue in business.
You have not tried it.

It has been tried in Nova Scotia, but without success. Now, hon. members refer to the experience of the banking system of the United States. In banking, as in a great many other enterprises, if a system is once instituted it is difficult to abandon it and immediately inaugurate a new one. The branch bank system of Canada is as old as confederation. I am not saying whether it is best or not, but I do say that it has fairly well provided for the necessities of the country in the past; in fact, I do not know what other kind of banking system could have prevailed in Canada. When one reflects that we have in this country a population of eight or nine millions occupying vast stretches of territory, one is forced to ask where the capital would have come from to establish in the cities and the towns and villages of Canada the banking offices that exist to-day, were it not for the branch bank system. I do not think it would have been possible; and whatever the defects of the system may be-and I presume it has defects-I say, nevertheless, that it has served Canada well.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has referred to the experience of small banks in the country. I remember in my own time, in the province of Nova Scotia, there were two local banks, which, I think, had not a single agency. Within the last twenty years they have gone out of business. And I might refer to other banks much more substantial, such for example as the Northern Crown, of Winnipeg. That bank merged with the Royal Bank either in 1918 or 1919. It was in a fairly liquid position, yet they found they could not safely loan their resources and protect their depositors and shareholders. They therefore had to go out of business. Nothing was said about the matter at the time; that particular merger was not criticized. But in banks, as in every other business institution, there is likely to come a time when the shareholders decide that they must liquidate or sell. And that very substantial bank, the Northern Crown, was obliged to do that. Or take the case of the Bank of Ottawa-a very strong institution, well entrenched in the Ottawa valley and with a splendid body of directors. A few years ago that bank found its position was in danger; at least, it could not sustain its position unless it spread out through the various provinces of Canada, which it had neglected to do in previous years. It was a bank in which a few persons were the principal shareholders, who thought they could not get additional capital by appealing to the public. And so

Bank Act
40S1
they declined to put further capital into the enterprise and in the end decided that it was better to merge with the Bank of Nova Scotia. The same thing happened in the case of the Bank of British North America, which was largely a Canadian bank without the shareholders' double liability. They had not established agencies throughout Canada in many places and they found the competition of the stronger banks, which had established themselves freely in all the provinces, so keen that they were obliged to sell.
There is one thing that may be said of the branch bank system which perhaps may be regarded as somewhat in the way of criticism: It makes it difficult for the small local bank to succeed. As the Minister of Finance has pointed out, however, we know very well that the small bank with local directors unfortunately succumbs to local influences, and too soon its resources are held by a few borrowers in the locality. And that is the difficulty. Under good management this might be avoided; but unfortunately our experience in the past only confirms this opinion.
Now, in these days, is $500,000 too much capital to require of a bank starting in business? It is no more than the equivalent of $200,000 or $250,000 ten years ago. A bank with just that volume of assets could not engage in a very heavy banking business even in a small locality. There might be considerable to say for the reduction of this minimum of $500,000; but the question arises, at what sum will you fix the minimum? Furthermore, is it wise to take the responsibility in view of the history of banking in Canada, and our experience in the past?
Again, there is the difficulty of obtaining good bank managers in Canada to-day. The present banks complain-they complained before the committee on Banking and Commerce-of this very matter. Further, I would point out that the small local bank will not receive deposits against the stronger banks doing business throughout Canada, and that is another consideration.

Would the hon. member
admit that the experience of the Weybum Securities Bank is an exception?-it has succeeded against the larger banks.
I am very glad to say that it is an exception. It is a small bank with seventeen branches.

It is operating under this
act.
Yes, it had the minimum capital of $500,000.
It is a small bank.

Yes, and I am glad to see that it is developing and becoming stronger. I only wish there were a great number of such institutions in the West. But there is this to be remembered in connection with the Weyburn Securities, it is a bank the shares of which are held by just two or three people, and I am informed that frequently they have had to come to the assistance of the bank. Then, the general manager has had an experience which peculiarly fits him for operating in the particular territory in which that bank conducts its business. That bank has great difficulty in earning dividends, and it is very important for a bank to earn dividends. Some hon. gentlemen across the way last night deplored the fact that in these days banks were paying dividends. As soon as a bank ceases to pay dividends, it ceases to do a banking business. You cannot compare a bank with an ordinary commercial business. Ordinary commercial corporations may suspend indefinitely the payment of dividends; but as soon as a bank fails to earn its dividends, its shareholders require the liquidation of the company in order to avoid the double liability; depositors will leave them, and for these and other reasons it is very important that banks earn dividends. I am glad, however, to express the hope that the Weybum Securities Bank will continue to do business in the West. It would be very desirable if it could be brought about that other banks of that size could be established in that area.
The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) suggested that possibly with a discount system in Canada, local banks might have an easier course to travel. There may be something in that, and probably the day will come when we shall have a rediscount bank in Canada, Then the establishment of local banks will perhaps, become a practical question. But there will always be this difficulty, that the small local bank will not be likely to have the kind of security which will be acceptable to rediscount banks; the better classes of securities will go to the stronger banks. I am not saying that in an absolute or dogmatic fashion. I might be wrong in that respect; but I think when we have functioning in this country an organized rediscount banking system, it is' just possible that local banks may successfully venture into the local banking business. The whole question is whether, in these days particularly when capital is timid, is it worth while to authorize the inauguration of banking business by banking companies with a smaller capital than $500,000. Personally, I do not believe that within the next five or ten years you could get
Bank Act

capital to engage in a purely local banking business anyway, except, perhaps, under exceptional circumstances such as prevailed when the gentlemen came over from the United States and started the Weyburn Securities.

There is a good deal of
force in the argument which the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has just put forward, as well as in that of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). I think the committee will realize and agree that in the past there has been a decided tendency towards mergers. I do not think any legislation that we can make will successfully combat that, because it seems to me a natural response to conditions generally. I agree also
4 p.m. that the present branch bank system has been peculiarly fitted to the conditions of a new country, and it is doing a very great service. I see also the force of the argument of the Minister of Finance that a small bank would, perhaps', have a great deal more difficulty in maintaining itself against the competition of larger institutions. But, at the same time, I do not think it is entirely wise for us to shut out small banks from making the attempt. In view of all these things, it is not likely that many will make the attempt -I think that is true. And so I would like to ask the Minister of Finance this question. In his opinion, what possible harm could come by reducing the amount required to start a bank, say, to $250,000? If no serious harm could be foreseen, would the minister entertain the idea of reducing the initial amount of capital stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would not think it was wise to induce people to put their money into a small bank. I think any money that is put into a small bank is not wisely invested, for the chances are that it will not be a successful institution. I think the amount of 8500,000 is not an excessive sum. May I say with regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) that I deplore, as he does, the fact that so many of our Nova Scotia banks have moved their headquarters to Montreal or Toronto? But I do not see how that can be prevented. I do not see anything in the Bank Act which created that situation, and I do not know of any provision in the Bank Act which could prevent it. It is one of the results of what I might call evolution under confederation. Many institutions which were prosperous in the Maritime provinces in the days before confederation are complaining to-day. I do not want to discuss the question of confederation; I simply state a fact. I remember when there were twenty wholesale houses

in Halifax all doing a prosperous business; to-day there is hardly one of them left. They have all been driven out by Montreal. As regards the banks which we had in Nova Scotia, the shareholders who built up the banks in that province found it convenient to sell their stock to other people. I have never found any complaint coming from the Maritime provinces as to this particular part of the act. There have been suggestions from other parts of the country that they would establish banks if they had the opportunity; but I never had any complaint from the lower provinces. And if they had an opportunity, I do not think any banks would be established in the lower provinces with a capital of less than $500,000, because their knowledge and experience of banking would satisfy them that the smaller institution could not have a fail chance in the competition for business.

I should like to say just one word in reply to a point raised by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean), that is about the Northern Crown Bank being amal- * gamated with another bank. I do not remember the particulars, but I understand this was a profitable venture for the people who founded that bank and afterwards found it wise to amalgamate. I suppose the same thing would apply to the Bank of Ottawa, and if I mistake not, the same thing would apply to the Bank of British North America.

I do not think it was a profitable sale for the Northern Crown because they had lost a great deal of their capital, and they had to furnish additional capital. The amalgamation was made after they found they could not succeed. It seems to me the hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Hudson) had something to do with that bank, and he might inform us upon that point.

I do not recollect the particulars altogether; but in a general way the shareholders of the Northern Crown, when they transferred their stock, as they did under the amalgamation agreement, got out just about what they put in. I think some of them may have lost a little in the way of premiums which they paid on their stock, but they certainly got out as much as they put in, apart from any question of premiums.

Just a word, Mr. Chairman, in regard to how this capitalization should be fixed. A lot of communities in Canada might be able to start a bank to take care of their local needs. Possibly none would

Bank Act
40S3
want to do so, but I do not think we should by this act forbid any community from embarking on such an undertaking. It seems to me less money has been lost in bank stocks in Canada in proportion to the total investment than in any other line. Possibly one of these small banks would fail once ;n a while, but I do not think such a failure would entail nearly as much hardship as the failure of one of our large banks. I do not think it is right for this committee to arbitrarily fix an amount of half a million dollars as the capital which must be subscribed. If any set of people want to invest their money in a bank with a smaller capitalization, I do not see why we should take it upon ourselves to prevent their doing so.
I cannot recall the particular section, but is it not a fact that a bank can start business with a paid up capital of $250,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is section 13.
Yes, but if I remember rightly the subscribed capital must be half a million dollars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There must be subscribers for half a million dollars, and they are liable to be called upon, but the bank can start iu business on $250,000. Surely that is low enough. It is hardly fair to speak of half a million dollars being necessary.
I trust the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) does not forget that there is a double liability clause attached to the stock.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That would be so in a small bank too.

Certainly, and if a smaller amount were fixed it would be that much easier to start the bank. I think the minister is a little too determined to prevent people starting a bank if they want to. That is the point in my mind. I think he is taking a wrong view. He might think that even a quarter of a million dollars is not a very large amount, but, as I said before, it might be really more than was necessary for a bank to function in some particular locality.

In regard to small banks, down in our province there is such competition for business among the chartered banks that as soon as it is thought the conditions warrant a branch is established in any village. I could cite cases where branches were established by the larger institutions for the benefit of the locality and the business offered was not sufficient to meet expenses, but the banks were willing to lose money in order to cater to the needs of the people. Where the banks are willing to meet every reasonable demand of the borrower, and also to take care of the deposits entrusted to them, I cannot see that any great advantage would be gained by the establishment of small, local banks, as there would be a greater risk to the depositors and the borrower would not get any cheaper money.

Criticism has been made in regard to the smaller banks because the managers and directors often get to know their clientele too well. I am afraid that this criticism does not apply to the present system of branch banks. I know of one locality where there have been six managers of the branch bank in the last ten years. It will be readily understood that under these circumstances, and with the directors residing about three thousand miles away, the bank has very little in common indeed with the localities where their branches are established. A few weeks ago we passed a Combines, Monopolies, Trusts and Mergers Act. It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that if we prevent competition by forbidding the establishment of smaller banks we are encouraging such combinations among the banking fraternity. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) referred to a sudden changing of the system. But the change would be very gradual indeed and business would not be upset in the slightest degree. It is simply a case of asking for a fair field and no favour. The criticism has often been made that more branch banks are not established because there are not sufficient local deposits to warrant their establishment. I should like to see that criticism confirmed by figures showing what deposits are placed in the banks in the Maritime provinces, the prairie provinces and British Columbia. We do not seem to have those figures given to us very readily. I think probably they would disclose that vast deposits are placed in the banks in those parts of Canada.
There is one other argument, and I think it takes some answering. We have two countries side by side, the United States with an independent banking system, Canada with a branch bank system. Both countries have many things in common, including vast-stretches of thinly populated country. One, however, has developed very fast indeed, the other has practically stood still. And, in the words of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good), the banking system in the United
Bank Act

States has had less failure on a percentage basis than the much-vaunted system of branch banks in Canada.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 22-Who shall be directors.
I beg to move that this section be amended by inserting after the word "election" in the second line the words, "but not less than a majority of the votes cast."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman explain that?

This House some months ago endorsed the proposition that members of the House be elected by a majority vote, and I think it is customary for the directors of any concern also to be elected by a majority vote. I simply ask by the amendment that what is generally recognized as good practice should be incorporated in this clause. I do not know whether or not there is any particular need for it, but the clause as it is leaves it quite open for the directors to be elected by minority votes. I do not think any possible harm can come from requiring the shareholders of a bank to see to it that they elect their directors by a majority.

A fair and equitable principle is involved in the proposal of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good), and I think it should meet with the approval of the committee and of the minister. No harm can be done by it; much good might result from it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have never heard of any trouble arising under this clause, and I do not think we need look round for any.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the amendment.

I think we ought to have a better reason than that.
Amendment (Mr. Good) negatived; Yeas, 23; Nays, 38.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 30-Appointment of officers, etc.

I should like to move that section 30 be amended by adding thereto, as subsection 4, the following:
4. Such officers, clerks and servants shall have and be deemed to have the right of association for all lawful purposes.
Under the Treaty of Versailles all employed persons are guaranteed the right to organize. Canada and this government are
[Mr. Spencer.
definitely committed to the principle of that clause of the treaty. The phraseology here is, I may say, taken direct from the tijeaty. In connection with a great many other institutions and organizations the right of employees to organize is specially recognized, and it seems to me it should be in this connection. We are here providing for various things- that the directors may appoint these officers and employees, may require of them certain bonds, and so on, and it is reasonable that the employees should be definitely guaranteed their natural rights. In this act we are giving special privileges to certain corporations. We are definitely recognizing the Bankers' Association, which is, of course, an association of employers. We are recognizing professional associations such as that of the accountants. There seems to be no reason whatever why we should not recognize that the employees should have the right to organize. At the present time the employees of the bank are absolutely at the mercy of their employers. If they should wish at any time to ask for an increase in their wages or a betterment of their condition their case is almost hopeless. I know that theoretically they Imay organize, but whenever that has been attempted it has been frowned down upon by the bankers, and the men who have attempted to effect the organization have been thrown out of their positions or transferre,d to other positions or prevented from receiving promotion. This is what actually takes place. I have had various representations made to me from bank men both in the West and in the East in regard to this matter.
Take the question of wages. I am informed that in some of the leading banks a great many of the clerks are receiving, to start with, some $350 a year. Sometimes that is supplemented by living quarters, and in other cases it is not. I am informed that in a great many cases the wages of bank employees amount to only $500, $600, or $700 a year. I received a rather pathetic communication the other day, since introducing this matter, from a young man who stated his position. He is an employee in a bank, married, with children, and is receiving only some $1,500 a year and finds it very, very difficult indeed to manage on' that.
Take, again, the question of marriage, and the conditions under which the bank clerks must live. We have the banks stipulating that a bank clerk may not marry until he has such-and-such a salary. That works out in practice, I am given to understand, that certain employees who have special friends among the bankers are able to obtain this privilege, while others are not able to do so. It seems as if any employer is going a very long way

Bank Act
indeed when he undertakes to dictate to his employee what his social condition shall be, whether or not he shall have the right to exercise legitimately the normal functions of manhood. These things are vital, and these conditions are very difficult to improve or alter unless you allow the employees the primary rights of freedom of speech and of association. I cannot see any good argument against such a clause being inserted. This was proposed in the Banking committee, and I am glad to know that the Finance Minister is favourable to its incorporation. I feel quite confident that a great many members of the House, irrespective of party, will feel in favour of definitely ensuring to the bank clerks that which all other people are supposed to enjoy.
Amendment negatived: Yeas, 23; Nays, 42.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 32-One vote for each share.

Before this clause carries, I would like to have an expression of opinion from the Minister of Finance as to the propriety of returning to a system of voting which, I understand, was in vogue in the banks some years ago, that is that there should be a limitation upon the principle of one share one vote. I think it is generally recognized among all co-operative organizations that the principle of one man one vote ought to prevail. The principle that is adopted in most joint stock companies is one share one vote. I have been informed that some years ago some of the Canadian banks voluntarily adopted a sort of compromise between the two principles so that some recognition would be given to manhood whether or not it was accompanied by dollars. I would like to have an expression of opinion from the Minister of Finance on this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whatever might be said in favour of the principle of one man one vote in the political sense, I think when it comes to money matters the old phrase "money talks" has to be recognized. I do not think it is reasonable to say that the man who owns only one share in a bank should have the same say as the man who has two. I think that is too chimerical.

I think my hon. friend has misunderstood me. I did not suggest that we should adopt the principle of one man one vote, but if a man had one hundred shares say, he should not be allowed voting power beyond that amount. There should be some limitation upon his voting power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think that can be done.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 54-Statement to be laid before annual meeting; liabilities; assets; other particulars; profit and loss account, etc.

I notice that in the
draft of the original bill the minister had two paragraphs, one called "appropriation account" and the other "contingent reserves, including undistributed profits." Would the minister explain why these two clauses were withdrawn?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After the bill was introduced we had many criticisms from all quarters. Whenever any suggestion was made that seemed to be reasonable I was very happy to concur in it. The suggestions made in regard to these paragraphs seemed to me to be reasonable. We discussed the matter in committee and the committee agreed to the changes as herein made.

May 1 ask the minister
if "from all quarters" included anybody but the Bankers' Association themselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh, yes. I had letters
and suggestions from various members of parliament, from outside citizens, suggestions came to me in a variety of ways. I think even the public press undertook to give me some advice in the matter.

Would the minister be good
enough to tell us why these amendments were put in the draft bill as first brought down? Was there not some good reason for having them inserted there?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It seemed to me at that time, in the best light we had, that the way there proposed was the best way to deal with them. Better light came to us and we acted accordingly.

I was just wondering if
the minister would tell us where the light came from?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I get light from various sources, occasionally from my hon. friends, and I am very glad to avail myself of it.

It seems to me
there should be a provision requiring an accurate statement to be made with regard to the value of bank premises. There is no such requirement in this clause. I should like to call attention to the evidence given by Sir Edmund Walker before the committee on Banking and Commerce.
He was asked:
Q. Are the figures that are given in the returns made to the Minister of Finance, showing the value of the ibank premises, exactly correct and complete?
Bank Act

He replied:
A. We tell our shareholders almost every year that our bank premises are entered at half their value, we tell them that our bank premises are worth twice as much as they are stated at in our statement in the first place, they are $7,236,000, in the last statement, those are the premises that the bank owns directly, the bank owns premises through a realty company as well-that is about half of the value of those particular premises.
Q. That is the value of the premises held by the Bank of Commerce is some 15 millions?
A. About 14 or 15 million.
Q. What was the purpose of holding bank premises in the name of a holding company?
A. We had to replace the landlord that I spoke of as existing throughout Ontario, but did not exist in the West. We created a realty company, and as we built our buildings we provided out of our currency profits for half the cost of the building, and took that in stock in the realty company, and wrote that stock off. This realty company mortgaged the premises of the bank for the other 50 per cent, and the bank rented offices from the realty company at a rental which in 20 years would amortize the last of the debt.
Q. What would be t^ie value of the holdings of your subsidiary realty company?
A. 8 or 10 millions. I think 10 millions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would call the hon.
member's attention to section 147b which provides for neglecting to make a return for the value of property. This seems to be a provision of the kind the hon. member has referred to.

And section
79 which calls for a return to the minister in regard to the value of real and immovable property.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There is section 147b
and section 79. In the former a penalty is provided for neglecting to comply with the terms of the section.

In paragraph (r)
of the clause we are now considering the statement of assets is required to show:
"bank premises, at not more than cost, less amounts (if any) written off."
It seems to me that, in some way, a fair valuation of the bank premises should be definitely required in this statement. If the statement is worth anything it should show the exact value both of the real estate held directly and that held through any holding company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Paragraph (r) provides
for a return of the bank premises.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is the one under discussion now.

It seems to me this matter
is one of very great importance. There was a good deal of discussion about it in the committee on Banking and Commerce and I understand the Minister of Finance took the

position then that so long as the real estate assets were not over valued no harm was done. I should like to dissent from that view. The banks are essentially public service corporations, and if the value of their real estate assets are written down, it is possible to conceal a very large amount of profits in those assets.

There is this
exception: Under section 79 the bank must every year make a return to the minister showing the fair market value of its real estate and property.

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I am
very glad the hon. member called my attention to that. There is that provision, but I think the House should also make provision for return in another place. Why should we not provide in the item in the clause we are now discussing that there should be a statement of the fair market value of the assets, and not have the banks possibly writing them down to a very small fraction of the real value?
I might call the attention of the committee to the other paragraphs, (m) and (n), which were withdrawn by the minister during the course of the consideration of the bill m committee. They are now hidden under a new (m) and (n)-"other current loans and discounts in Canada, after making full provision for all bad and doubtful debts," and "other current loans and discounts elsewhere than in Canada, after making full provision for all bad and doubtful debts." The point is whether or not the banks should be permitted to conceal the amounts which they have appropriated for bad and doubtful debts. I want to place myself on record as being somewhat doubtful of the decision which the committee reached in that respect, and of the propriety of following the suggestion made by the Minister of Finance in the first place that these appropriations should be disclosed in the statements.

It would be only fair to the shareholders to have the bank premises shown in the annual statement at their fair market value rather than as it is shown at present. This statement as it is made out now is misleading. I think the shareholders are entitled to know how much of the bank's money, capital or accumulated profits, has been put mto bank premises. I have here a statement issued by Dickinson & Walbank, of Montreal, in regard to the merger of the Merchants Bank with the Bank of Montreal, in which the following statement appears:

Bank Act
It is evident from the government reports and statements made at the meeting in February, that the entire capital of the Merchants Bank was in premises of the bank. In that case, the shareholders' equity, as shown above at $12,826,189 and $12,041,761, in December and January respectively, has against it a bonded liability on bank premises account, approximating $5,000,000 which must consequently be deducted, thus bringing the total book-value down to $7,041,761 or $67 per share, at the end of January.
In the bank returns of February 28 I observed that one bank with a paid-up capital of $15,000,000 gave its bank premises as being valued at $7,000,000, and the general manager of the bank, I believe, made the statement that the value shown is only 50 per cent of the cost of the premises. A lot of the profits or of the capital of the bank has been invested in bank premises and it is not shown in their annual statement, as it ought to be. This is misleading, and the Minister of Finance should amend paragraph (r) so as to show bank premises at their actual value or their fair market value.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 56-Shareholders' audit.

I have an amendment to offer. I move that section 56 be amended by adding thereto the following subsections:
(17)	Ths Governor in Council shall appoint a competent person who shall be an officer of the government with the title of Government Auditor, whose duty shall be to examine all reports of auditors made under this act and require all such auditors to report to him upon the adequacy of the procedure adopted by the bank for the safety of its creditors and shareholders, and as to the sufficiency of their own procedure in auditing the affairs of the bank, and he may enlarge or extend the scope of the audit, or direct that any other or particular examination be made or procedure established in any particular case, as the public interest may seem to require.
(18)	The Government Auditor shall have all the powers of inquiry with respect to the duties to be performed by him conferred upon commissioners appointed under the Inquiries Act.
(19)	The Government Auditor shall annually make report in writing to the minister of all examinations and inquiries made by and directed to be made by him and his finding and recommendations in respect thereto, and such report shall be laid before parliament within twenty-one days from .the commencement of each session thereof.
After the near-failure of the Merchants Bank there was a very general request by the public as voiced through nearly all our newspapers, that there should be some more definite government audit or inspection. The amendment submitted does not look to the appointment of auditors who will go over the entire work of all the banks. That would seem to me to be quite unnecessary, and of course it would involve an enormous expenditure. That is not contemplated at all. It
is proposed, though, that some one should be expressly charged with the responsibility of supervising the various bank audits and of seeing that they are standardized and are sufficiently wide in scope to cover all requirements and to bring to the notice of the minister, and subsequently of parliament, all the essential facts in the case. It has been objected by the bankers that the government is not in a position to audit the accounts of the banks, because it is not able to command the services of any one sufficiently competent for the purpose. I cannot see the validity of that objection, for the government of the country, charged with the responsibility of safeguarding the interests of the public and of the bank shareholders, should undoubtedly be able to secure the services of competent-men. Further than that, it has been objected that if the government undertook such an inspection it would assume a certain responsibility. Well, that is precisely the reason why such an inspection should be made. The government cannot avoid a very considerable measure of responsibility with regard to the banks. Under this bill which we are passing the banks are given special privileges. They have almost a monopoly of the credit system of the country and, besides, they enjoy the very valuable franchise of issuing currency. Under these conditions the public have a vital interest in all that transpires in the banks.
How can the hon. member say the banks have a monopoly when any group of persons with $500,000 can organize a bank?
If another group entered, the number of such organizations would be increased from seventeen to eighteen, and those eighteen groups would still have that monopoly.
And why not fifty or sixty groups? There is no monopoly when it is open to any other group to come in. There is no restriction to the number of banks that may be organized.

Since the hon. member raises this question I may point out that as a matter of fact, within -the last few years, instead of banks multiplying they have been reduced in number from thirty-four to seventeen; and that is a sufficient indication of the likelihood of other groups breaking into the ring. I repeat, there is virtually a monopoly on the part of the banks of giving credits to the people, and there is the further valuable franchise of the issuance of currency. Under these circumstances the government cannot escape its responsi-

Bank Act

bility, and it would seem that the best way of meeting the situation would be to appoint some one definitely who shall be given the responsibility of supervising the auditors. I fancy if this were done and if there was any weakness in any bank, it would be brought to the attention of the minister >n time to save the situation.
One other objection that I have heard alleged against this amendment, is that the business of a bank is private in character. Surely, sufficient evidence was produced in the Banking committee and on the floor of this House last night to show that essentially the banks of to-day are in the nature of public utility corporations. Their concerns are not entirely private. With the special privileges they are granted, with the franchises and charters they are given, they can no longer be considered as carrying on a private business. The public Is interested to a great extent; a section of the public as shareholders, another and larger section of the public as depositors, another and still larger section of the public as borrowers-those who technically make deposits and are given checking privileges;-these large sections of the public are tremendously interested in what is taking place. For these reasons, it is highly desirable that we should have an officer charged with keeping in close touch with the affairs of the bank, who would bring this information to the minister and to parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We had a very full discussion of this matter before the committee. The clauses which we have already passed or which we are about to pass give adequate powers and protection to the public in the matter of audit, and I do not think it is wise to ask us to go any further.

When this matter was under consideration in the committee, Mr. Edwards gave us some information about associations of auditors who met together from time to time to discuss methods, to standardize methods, and to confer over their work. He gave it as his opinion-and I think his
5 pan. opinion is certainly worth while noting-that this collaboration and conferring amongst auditors was very useful for them. It occurs to me that if a government auditor were appointed, as has been suggested in this amendment, he could very well function as a sort of presiding officer over those bank auditors who had been selected by the various banks to audit their affairs, and that in that capacity, as president or chairman, he would not in any way dominate the auditors, but he would bring them together to confer over their methods and he would

also, in his position of government auditor, be able to examine their methods and to report upon them regularly to the minister. In that respect too, he should be able to convey information to the department of any incipient difficulties that might be discovered in the banks' affairs.
There seem to me to be two advantages in this proposal, one the advantage of regularly reporting to the minister and to parliament, and the other, that of regular conferences- "get-togethers"-amongst the auditors. The latter advantage would, I think, very largely ensure better auditing methods, so that what has happened in the past to the Merchants Bank, as far as we have been permitted to get information on that affair, would be less likely to occur. The auditors who confer together amongst themselves and discuss their work are in a much better position to do good work than those who work in an isolated fashion. I think the suggestion is well worth considering. It would be comparatively inexpensive, and it is well worth while. I want, in conclusion, to call the attention of the committee to what the minister said in defence of turning down this proposal in the select standing committee. It has reference to the next clause 56A where it is provided that:
The minister may direct and require any auditor appointed under the next proceeding section of this act, or any other auditor whom he may select, to examine and inquire specially into any of the affairs or business of the bank, and the auditor so appointed or selected, as the case may be, shall, at the conclusion of his examination and inquiry, report fully to the minister the results thereof.
I should like to submit to the committee and to the minister that this is very inadequate, because the minister will not order a special inquiry until he receives some information of a serious or threatening character. He will not be on his guard unless he is receiving the information regularly. The door will be shut after the horse is stolen, and the expense will have to be incurred when it is too late to correct the difficulties and mistakes. By providing for a government auditor, one who may function as president of the bank auditors at regular conferences, you are going not only to get better service on the part of the auditors but also to ensure that regularly, once in every six months or once a year, the department shall be in receipt of a report from this government auditor upon the auditing methods. It seems to me very obvious that this is a wise provision. As I said, it is not an expensive provision at all; it probably would cost very little more than the special inquiries which the minister is empowered to make at any time.

Bank Act

Before this innocent amendment moved b'y the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) is finally slaughtered, I should like to say a word or two about it. It asks for government inspection of banks. The only thing that I do not like about it is that it asks the government to do anything. I am not very much enamoured of any proposal that places more responsibility upon government. I am in favour of government being asked to do just as little as possible: for two reasons. First, you are likely to get little from a government; second, no organized body is less capable of carrying things out in a practical way-I am not referring to the present government, I am speaking of all governments. However, this is one of the capacities in which the government might be able to act, namely, that of a policeman to walk up and down the country and club people when they violate a certain law. That is about all that is involved in this clause which is sought to be amended by my hon. friend. This has been the practice ever since governments were organized. I am in favour of the amendment. As to the right of the government to do this, there can be no question at all. As the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) said, this is one of the powers which the government, as the representative of the people, must exercise in its supervision of our banking system. Therefore, the government having the right to inspect the institution to see that it is doing what it was intended by the law to do, and being, as I believe, eminently fitted to act in the capacity of a policeman, I am in favour of this amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I think the proposal contained in the amendment cannot be as lightly dismissed as perhaps the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) would suggest. It seems to me that in the existing regulations of the Bank Act the government recognizes its responsibility in this matter by the minister being empowered, when he sees fit, to employ an auditor to investigate any bank. This amendment does not ask for a full-fledged system of government inspection, but for the appointment of a particular individual whose duty will be to do continuously what otherwise the minister under the statute can do from time to time- in the past always too late; a government auditor whose duty it is to examine the reports as they come in, as only an auditor can examine them, to ascertain any discrepancies there may be between these and former state-
261 i
ments, to keep, as it were, a watch on the bank's affairs from time to time through the medium of its statements and otherwise from information he can obtain under the powers committed to him by the proposed section- he is an eminently desirable official. In other words, you would have a watchdog on guard all the time comparing these various financial statements, dissecting them, calling for further statements if necessary, and so relieving the minister of that burden and perhaps, in some cases, ascertaining unfortunate circumstances before any harm was done. For instance, the Merchants Bank, of which we have heard so much, issued statements from month to month, all of which were false and fraudulent. That situation existed for a period of at least six or seven months. But how can you expect any employees in the Finance department to scientifically dissect a bank's financial statements and discover whether or not they contain any discrepancy, and whether or not any investigation should be made? It may be that a government auditor appointed in the manner suggested by the member for Centre Winnipeg would be able to disclose such a situation as existed in the Merchants Bank long before the failure took place, and the minister was called in as an undertaker to look after its affairs.

There would be a great
deal of force in the proposal of the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg and in the arguments of those supporting his amendment if no amendment had been made to the provisions of the old act. But this clause which we have under consideration is almost new. There have been some vital amendments made in it, and I consider that clause 56 is perhaps the most important and significant in the whole act so far as it relates to the practice of banking in this country, and having particular reference to the Merchants Bank case. As a matter of fact, the changes now presented to the committee in this bill cover completely the discrepancies in the old act. Let me just cite one or two. Under the old act there was one auditor under the control of the banks, without any limitation. In this amended clause we have two independent auditors appointed with a very strict limitation, and in addition, in subsection 9 of clause 56 and also in clause 56A, we have the minister specifically empowered to do exactly what this amendment asks to have done. The only difference between the amendment of the hon. member and the two provisions* to which I have referred is that his amendment calls for the setting up of an officer, while in these clauses the minister is
Bank Act

empowered to do all that the hon. member asks to have done.
Now, what I wish to impress on the committee is this-and it has certainly been very forcibly impressed upon my own mind-that by adopting the amendment proposed by the hon. member there is a danger that you make the minister, or the government, responsible for the accuracy of the bank audit. I do not think we are prepared to go that far. But under the provisions as they now stand are contained all the powers that are in this proposed amendment, only the sign of approval of the minister upon the audit to the public is not given. This is a difference and a distinction which I think is to the advantage of the public. Besides, the auditors report to the directors, and a copy of their report is then sent to the shareholders. All of this is more or less new. So I consider, Mr. Chairman, that in the amendment made by the committee to the clause as it stands we have safeguarded the various points raised in this dis^ cussion.
Amendment (Mr. Woodsworth) negatived.

Mr. Chairman, before the
clause carries I would refer the committee to subsection 9, where it says:
The minister may from time to time require that the auditors of a bank shall report to him upon the adequacy of the procedure adopted by tihe bank for the safety of its creditors and shareholders, and as to the sufficiency of their own procedure in auditing the affairs of the bank; and the minister may at his discretion enlarge or extend the scope of the audit, or direct that any other or particular examination be made or procedure established in the particular case as the public interest may seem to require.
It will be noticed that the minister himself is here proposing procedure under which he will incur this moral responsibility which on most occasions he apparently desires to evade as far as possible. It does seem to me that if the minister is going to have the auditors inquire into the affairs of the bank the inquiry should be made regularly before the bank comes under suspicion. I would move that subsection 9 be amended by prefixing thereto the following words:
The auditors shall report to the minister at least once in each year upon all loans exceeding five per cent of the paid up capital of the bank, and shall state specifically whether or not in their judgment such loans are adequately secured.
It does seem to me that if the shareholders' auditor would forward to the Minister of Finance a statement covering the loans exceeding five per cent of the paid up capital of the bank and state specifically whether or not in his opinion these loans are adequately

secured, we shall have taken a step toward safeguarding the interests of the banks.

How often
would that be done?
At least once a year.

What would
be the good of it if it was not done daily or weekly?

As a rule, loans run for
more than six months before they become bad. I will not attempt to urge that it is possible to safeguard a bank from bad management. But in the case of the Merchants Bank I think it could be demonstrated, if we had any investigation, that some of these loans had been bad for four years but were allowed to run on as current loans. If the auditor in the case of the Merchants Bank had been required to make a return of this kind to the minister it is possible that some of these loans would have been looked into before they got into such bad shape. There are a good many people in Canada who believe that the governments are behind the banks and that their deposits are guaranteed. That belief was expressed to me by a very intelligent woman about a week ago. I would not say that that opinion is prevalent, but it is held by some. I do not see why the Finance Minister should try so hard to evade responsibility. I think the people would like him to assume some responsibility if it would in any way help to secure the position of the banks and in that way, of course, to secure the depositors.

The hon.
member has stated that quite a few people feel that the government has something to do with the banks. Well, that opinion will grow if the view expressed by some members of this committee is repeated, here or outside; and that would be unfortunate. The banks have been referred to several times today as public institutions. In one sense that is quite correct, but if by that term is meant that the state have some interest in the assets of the bank or in its control, then I say it is not correct, and that it is an unfortunate term to employ. Now, what is a bank?
Did I use the term that the hon. member has suggested? If I did, I do not remember doing so.

No, I was not complaining so much about any expression used by my hon. friend as about those used by some other members of the committee.

Bank Act

Sir Edmund Walker in his
evidence indicated clearly that a bank is a public service corporation. Is that not so?

I suppose it
is a public service corporation, but I do not think it is one which must be controlled in all its operations by the state. Some hon. gentlemen seek to develop that idea, and I say it is not in the interests of the state or of good banking. The first thing we know some people will begin to think the state is the shareholder and the depositor. The shareholders own the capital; the business is done largely on the depositors' money. The shareholders are all free individuals; they may dispose of their stock at any time; the depositor may withdraw his deposits. So, provided that we set up every safeguard we can devise for the protection of the public in their relation to the banking corporation in all its activities, we have done about all we can. What good could be served by having a bank auditor make an annual statement to the Finance department setting forth a list of the loans equal to or exceeding five per cent of the capital stock of the bank? It would be of no value, because the condition of a borrower's loan with the bank changes in some cases every week or every month-at least every three months. Why not put the responsibility upon the directors and the manager? They are following the transactions of the bank daily; they are intimately acquainted with every detail of its operations. Now, a very important clause which forms part of this section is in the act for the first time.
It reads:
It shall be the duty of the auditors to report individually or jointly as to them may seem fit to the general manager and to the directors in writing any transactions or conditions affecting the well-being of the bank which are not satisfactory to them, and which in their opinion require rectification-
And so on. I submit that no better safeguard than that could be devised; the shareholders' auditors are required to sumbit in writing to all the directors any information respecting any account the condition of which they think may affect the welfare of the banking institution. After all, it is only those who audit frequently and who become intimately associated with the bank's methods of business who can audit properly. So I think the clause which I have read affords more protection than the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). I further submit that it is not necessary, at least at the present time, to interject any government official into the auditing of the banks' affairs.

Just a word in reply to the hon. member for Halifax. I would not like the committee to get the idea from what he has said that I was proposing in any way to interfere with what was proposed under subsection 10, providing for a report of the auditors to the directorate. I was simply trying to enlarge on that idea a little bit and am proposing that the return go to the minister. If the hon. member for Halifax were logical it does seem to me that he would object to subsection 9, as well as to my amendment, because under subsection 9 the minister is given power to have these auditors make a report and is assuming some responsibility in connection with the affairs of the bank. The reason, I think, that we attempt by legislation to exercise some control over the banks and their actions is because we give them very special privileges, and when we do that it seems quite proper that we should exercise some legislative control over them.
Amendment (Mr. Coote) negatived,

On section 60-Cash reserves in Dominion notes.

I would like the Finance
Minister to be good enough to explain the reason for requiring the bank to hold in Dominion notes not less than forty per cent of the cash reserves which it has in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a very old provision in the Bank Act. It really amounts to a loan which the banks make to the government; that is really the effect of it.
