speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not old enough to remember.
May I then press the question and ask the minister if he is not old enough to remember why it was originally put there, can he tell us why it is there to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is one of the little things which we exact from the banks. The banks to that extent loan that amount of money. They have to get that amount of Dominion notes, which is equivalent to loaning the money to the Dominion government. I think my hon. friend is not anxious to give the banks greater privileges.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

Bank Act

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On section 61-Issue of notes.

Just what
would be the advantage to the country?

The first advantage would be that the holder of a Dominion government note would know that the money it represented was as good as his country. A bank note, on the other hand, is of questionable value, or it might be. The next advantage would be that this country would secure an additional revenue of I think five or six million dollars a year if the banks were charged a rate of only three per cent. On what ground can the giving of this privilege to a bank be defended? In Australia the privilege of issuing notes has been retained by the government since the year 1910, and the banks in Australia seem to be able to function and to furnish the people with money at as low a rate of interest, and probably lower, than the 
banks charge in this country. I do not think that our banks are in any way making a return to us for this special privilege which they enjoy. I think some reason should be given, if there is any, why the banks should have this privilege of issuing notes. I might quote briefly from a pamphlet issued by Mr. Ward, of Winnipeg. He says:
A bank note is simply a promise to pay. If you want to borrow money from the bank and draw the cash you hand the banker your note, which is your promise to pay, and in exchange he hands you his notes, which are also promises to pay. The chief difference between them is that you have to pay interest on your note, but he pays none on his.
Exactly how much profit the banks make on their note circulation cannot be determined, as their method of accounting does not show this, but according to the figures furnished by the Commonwealth Bank of Australia, that bank has made something over two per cent profit on its circulation.
Has the Minister of Finance ever given consideration to the idea of the government issuing all the notes of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have given no particular consideration to that theory. I think the present system is working very well, and while I give consideration, perhaps not as much as I should, to all these financial propositions, I cannot say that I have ever thought it would be at all a desirable thing to deprive the banks of this privilege.

I should like to refer to a point or two, although I do not profess to understand very thoroughly the advantages to the state in issuing its currency as against its being issued by a bank, as in this country, I think that originally the right of note issue was given to the bank for good reasons. In the early days in Canada it was desirable that bank branches should be opened in the interest of the development of the whole country. If a bank's capital had to be invested in bonds, as is required in the United States, and they had not the right of note issue, they could hardly open up agencies. And the capital was not in this country at that time to carry on business in any other way. There is no doubt in the world that the right of note issue is of some advantage to a bank. At the same time it is of some advantage to the country, because our Canadian banks could not otherwise have had anything like the present number of agencies that they have opened throughout Canada.

Does the hon. member think we would be better off if there were fewer agencies opened?

Bank Act

That is another question altogether; possibly we would. However, we can never settle that question here, and I do not know where it can be settled. Ten years ago many of the representatives of the people in parliament were complaining that there were not enough banking facilities in Canada. Strange to say, with the passage of the last decade the complaint now is that we have too many banking agencies or offices, and there is some truth in it. But I do say that in the past, and at the present time as well, it has been of some advantage to communities to have branch banking offices opened as we have them to-day, and I do not believe it would have been possible without giving to the banks their present right of note issue. I admit it is of some advantage to them. Now, my hon. friend says it would be of some advantage to the state to issue notes. At the present time the country issues the one-dollar bill, the two-dollar bill, and the four-dollar bill, and up to the extent of $50,000,000 without requiring it to be covered by gold. In addition to that, we issue the copper and silver coin. Well, that is some advantage to the state, because we must always have till money and pocket money in circulation, and redemption is never demanded for this currency issued by the government; it is always outstanding, it can be issued freely without any fear of a demand for redemption ever being made. Above an issue of $50,000,000 our Dominion Bank Note Act requires there be dollar for dollar in gold, so if we took from the banks, say, the right of note issue of the $5 bill, under the terms of the Dominion Bank Note Act as it stands, we would have to put up gold to the extent of dollar for dollar. That is, the treasury would have to go out and buy $5 worth of gold, and against that they would issue the note and sell it to the bank. There may be some profit in it, but I do not quite see where it lies.
It what way would they buy?

They would
buy the gold in the gold market of the world where you can buy bullion or coin.
Does my hon. friend refer to the issue of notes under the Finance Act of 1914?

I am referring to the Dominion Bank Note Act which requires that all notes issued by the government, outside of $50,000,000, must be covered by gold, dollar for dollar. Of course, that provision has been modified by the Finance Act of 1914.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 64-Bank circulation redemption fund continued.

In regard to subsection 6, which provides that the circulation fund shall bear interest at the rate of 3 per cent per annum, it does seem to me rather an imposition to ask this country to pay interest on the circulation redemption fund. I would therefore move that subsection 6 be struck out. For this reason, Mr. Chairman: The banks are given the privilege of issuing notes to the amount of their paid-up capital. The privilege that they get there is surely worth the little bit of interest, they would lose on the money deposited with the government.
That is a cheaper rate than the rate at which the government can borrow money from the banks.
Yes, but the advantage to the banks of being able to issue their own notes will compensate for any loss they may sustain in this connection.

I wish to support the amendment. We have given the banks sufficient privileges without adding this one to the number. The circulation fund might well rest with the government without paying any such interest to the banks.

I shall support the amendment and will not occupy time unnecessarily by speaking in its favour.
Amendment negatived.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 76-Business and powers of the Bank.

I move an amendment to paragraph (d) of subsection 2 of section 76 by inserting after the word "bank" in the third line of the paragraph the following words:
Or any agent or other person acting on behalf of the aforementioned officers, managers, clerks or servants of the bank.
The intention is to safeguard as fully as possible the principle involved in the amendment which was carried by the committee. Owing possibly to an oversight in the committee and in the drafting of the original amendment, adequate provision does not seem to have been made for what I conceive to
Bank Act

be a legal possibility of brokers or agents of the managers or clerks securing these loans. That is the reason for the amendment I offer, which in no way affects the section.

I would ask the hon. member this: If any one lends to the agent of a man does he not lend to the man himself? The amendment is only an addition of words that in my judgment are absolutely unnecessary.
The words may not be absolutely necessary, but as they do not in any way alter the principle involved they can do no possible harm, while I think they may do some good.

The hon. member might
suggest the words "directly or indirectly." They would probably convey the same meaning, while they have the merit of brevity.
That refers only to security.

I do not think the words proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Garland) are needed. As the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Baxter) has pointed out, the section as it stands now would cover any application for a loan or any loan actually made.

Further, how is the bank
to know in all cases that it is lending to an agent for a principal?

I think this
is only another example of the futility of trying to legislate against all possible evasions of an act, and such meticulous nicety can get you nowhere.

The hon.
member, I think, is imagining futility before he has proof of it. I suggest that we allow the words to be inserted, because, as I have stated, they can do no harm and they may do some good. I am ready to accept the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Parent), and I would propose the words "directly or indirectly" in substitution for what I have already submitted.
On the principle suggested by the hon. member there would be no reason why the Ten Commandments should not also be inserted: they can do no possible harm and they might conceivably do some good.

Would the
words "directly or indirectly" be satisfactory to my hon. friend (Mr. Garland)?
Yes, provided they are inserted in the proper place.
Will the hon. member answer my question first? Is he satisfied with the words "directly or indirectly?"
Yes.
Well, they are there now.
Where?

At the top of the subsection:
Except as authorized by this act, the bank shall not, either directly or indirectly.

Yes, but
they are not included in subsection (d).

Oh, yes; you
read them into subsection (d).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the hon. member desire to drop his amendment?

Yes, Mr. Chairman, I might as well. I desire to move a further amendment to the subsection 3. The subsection now reads:
3. No agent or manager of any bank shall act as agent for any insurance company or for any person in the placing of insurance, nor shall any bank exercise pressure upon any borrower to place insurance for the security of such bank in any particular insurance agency, but nothing herein contained shall prevent such bank from requiring such insurance to be placed with an insurance company which it may approve.
I move to amend this by adding after the word "bank" in the third line the words, "nor any officer or employee of any bank." In the last line of the subsection I would have all the words deleted after the word "placed." The intention of the first insertion is obvious. The deletion of the last words I recommend' to the committee because otherwise there would continue a practice that now prevails of discrimination against the mutual insurance companies; and we know only too well in western Canada that a grave injustice has been done to these companies in this regard. When you go into a bank to secure a loan, we admit, the bank is right in asking you to take out insurance upon your crop or upon whatever the loan may be given. But we do not admit the right of the bank to state in what company the loan insurance shall be placed. You are giving them that full right in this, to the detriment, I say, of the mutual insurance companies.

Supposing a
bank was interested in an insurance policy to be placed by way of security against a loan,

Bank Act
or insurance against loss of property pledged as security for a loan, surely the lending party, in this case the bank, would have the right of saying, for instance, that they would not allow that insurance to be placed in a company the solvency of which was very much doubted. That is the purport of this clause.

I would not object to that idea in the least, but I say that this clause, as at present drafted and under the present practice of banks in western Canada, will react against the interest of the mutual insurance companies. We are very anxious to develop the mutual insurance companies, and this will work an injustice upon them.

I have had a little experience with this proposal as outlined by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland). I remember some years ago when I was doing business with a bank, that if I went into the bank in the spring and asked for a loan, the manager of the bank would say to me:	"Yes, I . will give you a
loan, but you must put hail insurance on your crop." The effect of that was that the manager acted as agent and he collected the commission. If you were not willing to put on hail insurance through the particular company that he was representing, the manager would invariably turn down your application for a loan, no matter in what financial circumstances you might be. I could give the committee many cases where-

This is exactly what the Banking committee wrestled with and corrected in this clause. If the hon. member will read the first part of the clause, he wiil see that it covers all this.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Section 76, subsection
3. The question is on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it has been shown by the discussion, Mr. Chairman, that what the mover of the amendment is aiming at is already covered by the section as it stands.

When we ros,e at six
o'clock, Mr. Speaker, I was discussing the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) and was attempting to point out certain restrictions that I believe should be imposed on branch bank managers acting as agents for insurance companies. I have some information in regard to this particular matter that I know to be correct. Some five or six years ago branch bank managers used to act as agents for hail insurance companies, and many farmers desiring to get loans had to place their hail insurance with the company represented by the bank manager before any accommodation was granted them. A year or two later the bank accountant took the place of the manager as insurance agent. Under these conditions we can well understand that it is not in the best interests of the banks themselves that this practice should continue, for I know of many farmers who because they placed their hail insurance as required by the bank's officials received loans which they were not entitled to, while other farmers, not desiring to place their hail insurance through the particular company represented by the manager or accountant of the bank, were refused the accommodation that they were justly entitled to. Therefore it is necessary to include in this particular section any employee of the bank, otherwise some employee will merely become agent for the manager, and I think this part of the amendment should be accepted.
With regard to the latter part of the amendment, to delete all the words, "with an insurance company which it may approve," I think this also should be accepted. We find that many managers of branch banks in the West discriminate against mutual insurance companies. We have some very fine mutual companies in western Canada, and the branch bank managers, usually being interested in one of the ordinary line companies, refuse to accept insurance in these mutual companies.

Is it not a
fair condition for anyone to require that an insurance policy shall not be carried in a mutual company? Many people do not desire that insurance in which they are interested
409b
Bank Act

shall be taken out in a mutual company. Surely it is not fair to force them to accept #uch insurance? i There are many strong mutual companies, but on the other hand many of them are doubtful-some are not even that.

In reply to the hon. member, I would say that we have many sound mutual companies in western Canada. But whether they are sound or not makes no difference to the branch managers, they object to the insurance being placed through these companies. The municipal Hail Insurance Company of the province of Alberta is to all intents and purposes a mutual company, and it is one of the strongest hail insurance companies in the province. This organization is really composed of the rural municipalities in Alberta. It carries about 55 per cent of the hail insurance in that province, and the rates are much lower than those charged by the ordinary line companies. Its operations have been very successful. Moreover, this organization gives its insurance on time; the rate is not set until the losses are known in the fall. The rate is applied as a tax on the land, consequently the security is of the best. Our branch managers, of course, object very strongly to that class of insurance, notwithstanding the fact that it enables the farmer who cannot pay for insurance on his crop in the spring to get the insurance on time, and to get it at cost, the rate being considerably less than that at which the line companies can carry the risk. I therefore suggest that the amendment proposed by the member for Bow River should be accepted. It would be in the interests of the banks themselves, and I am satisfied that it would be in the interests of the farmers of western Canada.

I think the amendment
should receive the support of the committee.
I happen to be secretary-manager of a mutual hail insurance company in Saskatchewan. In fact, I, in company with a few others in Saskatchewan, jvas the first to start a mutual hail insurance company in that province.
I believe there are two such companies in existence now. Some years ago the banks were quite willing to accept our insurance as collateral security, but during the past few years some bank managers or accountants have become agents for various other companies and have refused to accept our insurance; they will only lend money to the farmers to buy insurance in the companies they represent. To that extent it seems to me they are catering to the capitalistic com-
panies and, in another respect, are endeavouring to destroy any mutual arrangement we may make among ourselves for our own protection. We need to encourage co-operation among the farmers, and this is but one instance of co-operation. I may give a little history in regard to our company: Where the line companies have a 6 per cent rate or an 8 per cent rate where there is a note, during the last six years the company I represent has paid every loss in full and has at no time charged a higher average rate than 3 per cent. In one year when we had a heavy loss we charged 4 per cent, but in other years we have charged as low as li per cent. We have carried that insurance; we have paid all losses. It does seem to me that this clause gives the banks and their agents an opportunity to discriminate against mutual insurance. I feel sure that in this regard we should have the support of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), who believes in co-operation. I trust that this amendment will pass, not simply because it comes from this side, but because it will give a fair deal to our mutual insurance societies in the West. I hope the committee will see to it that there is no discrimination against any mutual hail insurance company organized among the farmers for their own protection.

I am fully in sympathy with this amendment. The mutual insurance companies out West are certainly doing good business, and they are making it possible for a great many people in the rural districts to carry insurance that otherwise could not afford to carry insurance. No one should be under an obligation to insure with the banks; in fact, it should be against the law for the banks to require that to be done. However, it was not on that point that I rose to say a few words. I think this government would be well advised to appoint a commission of. say, three persons to look after the bank interests and banking generally in this country. I would suggest that one member of the commission be appointed by the government, one by the banks themselves, and the third possibly by the prairie farmers. As it was brought out in the evidence before the Banking committee, that it is by them that credit is most needed, I think a commission of that kind could do good work. They might be empowered to prevent the duplication of banks in small villages and thus go a long way toward reducing the costs of the banking system. I know certain locations where there are three banks but not enough work for one. If the banks and branches were charged a

Bank Act
license, such a commission as I suggest could exercise control by being able to cancel the license at any time when in their opinion there were too many banks, or to prevent a bank being started in a place where one was not needed. If it is possible in this way to reduce the expenses of the banks in the outlying districts, the banks would be given a chance to make loans at a lower rate. I am not moving an amendment to this effect, but I think it is something that ought to be considered by the government.

The purpose of the section as it now stands is to prevent any agent or manager of a bank from acting as an insurance agent; he is prohibited from collecting insurance. This is a new section. The principle involved is very doubtful, as was suggested by some hon. members in the committee. However, the committee decided to adopt the clause, and that, I presume, is satisfactory to hon. members here; at least, there is no objection to it.
What is implied in the word "agent"?

A man who is carrying on or conducting a business at any place on behalf of a bank; a man who represents a bank as agent or manager. The latter part of the clause enables the bank to give its approval or disapproval of any insurance which has to be written and in which they are interested. Well, you cannot very well take that power from a bank. If I were lending money on real estate I would insist that the borrower insure the premises upon which the money was being lent. It is only fair to leave to the bank the right to insist that the insurance be placed in a solvent company. The mortgagor may want that insurance placed in a company which the public generally know to be insolvent or the solvency of which at least is doubtful. You cannot take that right away from a man, and it should not be taken away from a bank.
We have heard something about the mutual hail insurance companies in the West. I know nothing of them. Mutual insurance companies may be very strong to-day, but when they fail they are gone, they are no good, and they do frequently fail. I remember when I was a boy there were mutual marine insurance companies in the province of Nova Scotia. They were quite a common thing, but none are to be found to-day. So long as mutual insurance companies can pay their liabilities they are all right, but when they fail to do that, they are no good. They are not as good as the old line insurance companies as a rule, especially when those old line companies have built up a reserve. But what I say is that the first part of the section effects the intentions and desires of the special committee and apparently meets with the approval of this committee. The latter part of the clause leaves with the bank that is interested in any insurance that is to be placed the right of approving or disapproving of the company selected. Now can that right be fairly taken away from a bank? It cannot be taken away from the ordinary individual engaged in busniess, and if the principle is sound in the one case I think it is sound in the other. I think the committee should adhere to the section as it stands.

I wish to say a few words in regard to a matter that was brought to my attention in the West some time ago. For example, a man received a very large loan from a bank and gave as security a great many farms that he happened to own. In consequence of not being able to pay this loan the bank took over and worked those farms themselves. They took everything the farms produced and then absolutely refused to pay the taxes. They had the farms, they had the produce which came from those farms, but they refused to pay the taxes. I say the banks should not be allowed to enjoy this power. They should not be allowed to take a man's property and everything it produces and refuse to pay the taxes incurred.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Subsection agreed to.
On section 91, subsection 1-Interest at 7 per cent may be charged.

This subsection received very
lengthy consideration in the special committee, but the matter is of such importance that I think it merits further consideration by this committee. The first question which naturally occurs to one when approaching a restrictive interest clause is whether or not it is proper to have such a clause in the act. I am frank to confess that if the law of supply and demand operated, and the forces of competition were actively at work, there would be little value in a section of this character. I recall that the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in the discussion of the principle of this clause before the special committee harked back to the Middle Ages in
order to get some comfort for his view that such a restriction should not be imposed. He called to his aid Bacon and, strange to say, he also placed great reliance on the remarks of Adam Smith, although just why he singled out that great political economist as an authority on this particular subsection alone is rather difficult to understand. However, it is perfectly clear that Bacon wrote long before the days of organized banking, and Adam Smith wrote many years before the industrial revolution in England changed the whole industrial and economic fabric, before the day of mergers, trusts and other combinations of capital which have largely resulted in monopoly.
There can be no doubt that at the present time our banking system is a monopoly. This parliament has created certain corporations to which are delegated the business of banking, and it has prohibited all others from engaging in the business except on compliance with certain conditions'. Unless a corporation has received the imprimatur of this' parliament and has complied with the provisions of the Bank Act it cannot carry on a banking business. I disagreed with the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) this afternoon when he practically suggested that a banking corporation stands in exactly the same position as any other corporation. A banking corporation is a public service institution. It was so stated by Sir Edmund Walker before the special committee, and he is perhaps one of the greatest of our authorities on banking. Such a corporation derives' large monopolistic and special privileges from the people of Canada, including the privilege of issuing bank notes, which is of great value to it from a financial point of view. A banking corporation, to my mind, is in substantially the same position as a railroad corporation. The latter must comply with the provisions- of the Railway Act in detail, and under that act the rates which it may charge for the transportation of passengers and freight are . egu-lated by our Board of Railway Commissioners. When one has in mind the monopolistic nature of the business and the conditions which exist to-day in the way of mergers and combinations of capital, it is reasonable to urge that a maximum interest rate should be fixed. I do not say that the rate chargeable on a particular transaction should be determined, but certainly a maximum controlling interest rate should be established. Parliament has recognized that principle for many years. Not only do we fix a maximum interest rate in the Bank Act, but in the Interest Act we fix what we call the legal rate; in the Pawnbrokers Act we fix the maximum interest charge which can be made by a pawnbroker, and similarly

Bank Act

in the Money Lenders Act. So I say that regardless of how we may view the principle, under the circumstances it is essential that a maximum rate be fixed. That brings me to a consideration of the present section in the Bank Act. This section has been in the Bank Act for many years in a similar form. One would think from a casual reading of the provision that it was very clear and very definite that the bank could not exact a higher rate of interest than 7 per cent. But the section as it stands is burdened by a decision of the Privy Council which gives an altogether different interpretation to it. The case I have in mind was decided, I think, in 1913, immediately prior to the last revision of the Bank Act; I believe it was referred to in the discussion at that time. In that case the Privy Council held that the bank might charge any rate that it could agree upon with the borrower, notwithstanding the provisions of section 91. They held also that as the borrower knew that the charging of an excessive rate was illegal, he was therefore estopped from recovering back any amount in excess of the , fixed rate. So that the section, although apparently clear in its wording, means something altogether different from what that wording indicates. The section has no teeth at all; it simply provides a smoke screen behind which the banks can charge excessive rates. In the case to which I refer it was also decided that if a bank charging a rate of interest in excess of the statutory rate, sought to recover, it would be able to recover only 5 per cent per annum, the legal rate. But the banks, in order to prevent any possibility of recovery back, and any possible loss, discounted the notes in advance so that the borrower was estopped from setting up any claim to the excess interest charged. Now, that is the situation in regard to the present section. It is ineffective for the purposes for which it was framed. It is useless; it is simply a deception; it is a camouflage which permits the banks to charge any rate upon which they can agree with the borrower.
Now, the section has been abused. As I suggest, the banks, in order to get round the section, have charged discount rates in advance. It was brought out in an investigation conducted in -Alberta a year or so ago that there was apparently some understanding among the banks with regard to this discount rate. Where previously there had been no arrangement regarding this practice, it appears that within the last year or so the banks have universally adopted the practice of discounting. That practice is very objectionable indeed to borrowers; it simply means that when a borrower goes to a bank for $100

and gives a note for that amount, he will probably get-I am speaking of Alberta at the present time-$91, and then at the end of the three months' period he will be called upon to pay the full $100. In other words, it simply means taking the interest in advance.
That would be at the rate of about 36 per cent. My hon. friend must mean 9 per cent per annum.

Yes; I thank my hon. friend for calling my attention to that. I mean at the rate of 9 per cent per annum; the result would be that the borrower would get the amount he applied for, less $2.75. In addition, the banks have followed the practice of compounding the rates of interest. That is not particularly objectionable except when a high interest rate is charged, in which event, as hon. members will appreciate, the interest amounts to a very substantial sum indeed. The banks have charged very high rates of interest in the western provinces. I do not know what the situation is in eastern Canada. I understand that practically all loans there are made at the rate of 7 per cent or less, and that ample money is available to borrowers at that rate. In western Canada, within my memory at least, we have never been able to borrow money from the banks at less than 8 per cent per annum, unless, perhaps, in the case of a few choice and favoured borrowers. During the last two or three years, which have been years of considerable stress in the western provinces, the rates have increased. The rate of 9 per cent is very common; 10 per cent is by no means uncommon, and I am sure that hon. members from the western provinces can give many instances in which 12 per cent has been charged. There can be no question, therefore, that excessive interest charges are made in that part of the country to-day. It may be that eastern Canada is more or less indifferent as to this particular interest rate section. I readily appreciate that an easterner will not understand the situation, when he is called upon to pay only the maximum rate fixed by the act, or perhaps even less. But I suggest to the committee that in the West the burden of an excessive interest rate has been felt very heavily for many years. I am sure the committee will not tolerate a condition under which the West feels that it is suffering unduly through an economic exploitation, in this regard and in regard to other matters as well-an exploitation which seems to work in favour of the East alone. What is needed is an effective interest section in the Bank Act, a pro-

Bank Act
vision that will mean something to the borrower, a provision that will be a real safeguard to him and that will not allow the banks to exploit him at their pleasure. It is with that purpose in mind that I propose to move an amendment to this section. When in committee I moved an amendment somewhat more drastic in its character. I have tempered the amendment to some extent, and I trust that the members of this committee may give it favourable consideration. I do not propose to deal with subsection 2. The amendment which I propose and now move reads as follows :
That subsection 1 of section 91 be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
(1)	The bank may stipulate for, take, reserve, or exact any rate of interest or discount but not exceeding 7 per cent per annum and may receive and take in advance any such rate.
(2)	The rate of interest or discount charged by the bank shall appear on the face of the note, bill or other evidence of debt.
(3)	In the event that a greater rate than 7 per cent per annum has been paid to the bank, then the person by whom it dias been paid or his legal representative, may recover in any court the excess interest thus paid, provided such action is commenced within two years from the time such excess interest was paid.
(4)	In any suit, action or other proceeding concerning a bank loan wherein it is alleged that the amount of interest paid or claimed exceeds the rate of seven per centum per annum, the court may reopen the transaction and take an account between the parties, and may, notwithstanding any statement or settlement of account, or any contract purporting to close previous dealings and create a new obligation, reopen any account already taken between the parties, and relieve the person under obligation to pay from payment of any sum in excess of the legal rate of interest and if any such excess has been paid, or allowed in account, by the debtor, may order the bank to repay it, and may set aside either wholly or in part, or revise, or alter, any security given in respect of the transaction.
I would point out that the amendment does not affect subsection 2 of section 91 at all. In other words I have endeavoured to draft a clause Which I firmly believe is an effective controlling clause as far as the maximum interest rate is concerned. I have endeavoured to give to the borrower who has been charged an excessive rate of interest the right of action to recover back the excess charge, and I have also sought to give the court power in the event of a transaction being reopened to revise the transaction and adjust the rate of interest, at the legal rate which is five per cent per annum.

May I ask the hon. member, apart from the political aspect of such a proposal, does he think that on sound economic grounds it is practicable to fix a maximum rate of interest on capital or money in the
banks and leave the rate of interest on all other forms of money entirely unlimited?

My hon. friend is not altogether right when he suggests that all other obligations are left unrestricted so far as the rate of interest is concerned. I have already indicated to the committee that restrictions .will be found in the Interest Act, in the Pawnbrokers' Act and in the Money Lenders' Act.
But those only apply to amounts of two or five hundred dollars and the like. That is to stop the sixty percenters. That is not in the ordinary course of business.

I am not so sure that it js not done so frequently in the ordinary course of business. The legal rate of interest is fixed in the Interest Act, and that is a matter we are concerned with every day. As I say, Mr. Chairman, my object is to present to the committee an effective interest section. I am not wedded to the rate mentioned in the amendment, and if any reasonable argument can be advanced why that should be increased by a very moderate amount not over one per cent, I would be quite prepared after some consideration perhaps to agree to such an increase if the argument warranted it. But I think we should either have an effective section or no section at all.

I quite agree with the hon. gentleman who moves the amendment that this is a very important section. It was the occasion of a great deal of discussion and comment in the Banking committee, and I have no doubt that it is usually the subject of a great deal of discussion in the western provinces, where the discount rate is higher than it is in the East. That is not an unusual thing because in new countries the interest rate is always higher than in older countries.	You go to the
western states and you will find there a very much higher rate of interest than you do in the eastern states. You will also find in the American states that as they grow older and become more settled, as they advance in mixed farming and mixed products the rate of interest gradually falls. That, of course, is due to the fact that as the settlements become older there is an increase in accumulated wealth.
I agree also with the hon. member that the section is not in a very satisfactory state. Personally I do not like to see stated in a section that a given rate of interest shall be recovered, and yet it is possible for the banks by a system of discount, quite lawful, how-
Bank Act

ever, to recover a greater rate of interest than that stated which may be recovered at law. However, a problem was confronting the legislators of the day who framed that section, and I suppose it represents the best that could be done at the time. Personally I think it would be better and sounder if there was no reference at all to the rate of interest in the Bank Act. After all money is much like everything else. It should carry its market value. If in 1919 the Canadian banks in the East had raised the rate of interest to eight or nine or ten or fifteen per cent at a certain time, we would have escaped a great deal of the deflation that occurred and would have avoided the effects of the deflation from which we afterwards suffered. The American banks have been criticized by the most eminent bankers and economists of that country for not increasing their rate of interest in 1919. The American Federal Reserve Bank in 1919 was charging only 4| per cent instead of charging 6 per cent and over, and had that higher rate been charged the United States would not have suffered from the great deflation which afterwards occurred, much to their detriment. The same thing occurred here. The leading economists of the world say that the best way to control the level of prices is to put up the interest rate when inflation is on and prices are rising, and to reduce it when the reverse is the condition. I believe that is sound doctrine. I could quote to the committee this evening, if time permitted, a statement from, I think, the most eminent economist of the world to-day who, writing upon the control of price levels, says that the only practical way of doing it is by putting up or lowering the interest rate.
May I ask the name of the economist referred to?

Gustave Cas-sel, of Sweden. However, I am not going to propose that the clause in question be struck out; it would be very much resented, I suppose, by a very large section of the committee. The section in its present state is not perhaps quite acceptable to me; at least I do not care to see the provisions of the law stated in that way. However, it is perhaps better that there be some reference to the rate of interest which banks may charge.
The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) says there is no competition in banking. I say that statement is not correct. In money there is greater competition than anything in the world because there is absolute free trade in it. Millions of dollars come to Canada from the United States every year.

In normal times millions of dollars come from Great Britain. Money can flow into this country without any legal impediment, without any tax whatever; and if there is one thing in the world that is absolutely free from monopoly it is money.
Oh, oh.

My hon.
friends laugh but I venture to say they cannot contradict that statement.
I think so.

The hon. member for Calgary West compares money with a railway, and he says the railway is a monopoly. Well, the railway is a monopoly. It always was, because it has not been the custom of the country to let people build railways anywhere and as they liked. The public must be protected. Therefore before any corporation can construct a railway they must receive permission in the form of a statute from the state. There is a monopoly in that, but I say again there is no monopoly in money, there is no semblance of it.
Mr. hon. friend (Mr. Shaw) seeks to affirm that there is a monopoly in banking because the rate of interest is the same in specified areas. That is true. Take the British market, the freest money market in the world. The rate all over England is the same any one day in the week, and that rate is effective among forty-five millions of people. The rate in Paris is the rate all over France on any given day. The rate in New York is probably the rate in the eastern sections of the United States for commercial loans. The Chicago rate may be the effective rate in the middle western states, or in a certain area, and on the other hand Seattle, Portland, and San Francisco may fix the current rate on the Pacific. The rate in the West, of course, is higher than it is in the East, and I suppose there is a reason for it. I suppose there is a reason for the city of Calgary to-day, by authority of a statute of the province of Alberta, charging interest on overdue taxes to the extent of two-thirds of one per cent compounded monthly. I do not know what that amounts to, but that is what they do in the very city from which my hon. friend comes, and by authority of the legislature of Alberta.
My hon. friend will realize that is not an interest rate, that is a penalty.
Well, penalty rates are always well within interest rates.

No.

Bank Act
There is no use exacting penalty rates which will take the property away from the taxpayer.
That is what is happening right along.

In the West today the rates on private loans, as between individuals, are, I am told, far in excess of the rates charged in the East as between private individuals. I venture to say that if any of the hon. members from Alberta across the way were money lenders in that province they would exact 8, 9 and 10 per cent, and once in a while for very proper reasons would exact probably 10 or 12 per cent. Mortgage corporations charge a higher interest rate in Alberta and Saskatchewan than they do in the eastern provinces. I need not argue the reasons for that, they are very obvious. As I said before in new districts where there are no accumulations of wealth, where investment capital must come from a distance, higher rates of interest will be charged. Now, there was before the committee on Banking and Commerce-

If, as my hon. friend suggests, money flows freely from one country to the other, or from one province to another, wherever the market for the money is good, how does it happen that it never flows sufficiently into the money market to equalize the interest rates between the East and the West? How does it happen that the interest rates in the western and middle states in the United States are always higher than they are in the eastern states if money flows freely? Will my hon. friend kindly explain that?

Money flows from Canada into the United States almost daily because there are attractive investments there. The interest rate is better than they can secure in the investment market in Canada, and the security is satisfactory to the investor. The reason why the rates are higher in the middle and western states and in western Canada is because the security offered for investment is not so satisfactory to lenders or to investors. There is no class of securities that can be quickly cashed, there is no market in which they can be sold daily, and that is the reason why investment rates are usually higher in the West than in the East.
In that case Mr. Cassel and the hon. gentleman had better remove their argument from interest to security.
One governs the other.
I shall be quite content to stand by any opinion that Mr. Cassel expresses in preference to any view enunciated by my hon. friend.
May I interject here that I agree with the hon. gentleman in that regard, and I would much rather have the opinion of Mr. Cassel than that of my hon. friend.

I admit that is a very fair statement, and I am so modest that I would have made it myself without being encouraged to do so by my hon. friend. The interest rate in the West is, after all, a practical question. Reference was made to-day to the Weyburn Security Bank, a bank operating in the province of Saskatchewan, with seventeen agencies. The general manager of that bank is Mr. Powell. He appeared before the committee on Banking and Commerce and was asked as to what would be the effect if the bank interest rate was fixed at 7 per cent, and I want to read that portion of his evidence. The question was put to him by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens):
I would like to ask you three or four questions as to matters which are in the bill now or on notice of motion. From your experience in the West, what would be the effect upon your business as a banker if the rate of interest was fixed by law at say 7 per cent?
A. We would go out of business.
Now, I say to this committee: The manager of the Weyburn Security Bank is a practical man, an experienced banker, and I should say * an honourable gentleman, and I do not think he would make that statement if he did not honestly believe it, and did not feel confident the actual situation justified the answer made. The same question was put to-

May I interrupt to ask the hon. gentleman a question on that point? The hon. member ascribes to the manager of the Weyburn Security Bank certain attributes which I think are warrantable. Would he not ascribe similar attributes to those who presented the case for the western farmer? If he would, does it not then amount to a question as to whether agriculture is to be catered to, or the banks' interests are to be considered?
I do not quite apprehend the purport of the hon. member's question. Who particularly presented the case of the farmers before the committee apart from the members of the committee?
Exactly.

I failed to observe any desire on the part of the members
Bank Act

of the committee: from the western provinces to indicate by argument or by the presentation of facts, anything which would go to show that the banks could do business in western Canada under 7 per cent.

The hon. member misunderstands me. We did not attempt to prove that the banks could do business under 7 per cent in western Canada. We did state, however, that under present conditions agriculture could not continue to exist in western Canada at 8 per cent and over. That is the point.

Hon. members talk about interest rates being 9 and 10 per cent in the West. I want to point out that the evidence before the committee was to the effect that these rates did not generally prevail. Many loans are raised at 6, 7 and 8 per cent.
Did Mr. Powell state what the . average rate of interest charged by the bank was?

I think he did. He said that the average interest rate was about 9 per cent. That is what he said. Sir John Aird, the general manager of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, was also questioned upon this particular point. Probably there is no bank in Canada that has had so wide and extended an experience in the loaning of money in western provinces as has the Canadian Bank of . Commerce. This question was put to Sir John Aird by the hon member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael):
Q. That is a point I wish to get at. If the interest rate were kept strictly at seven per cent or below, you think your dividends would have to decrease to three per cent?-A. We would withdraw from a great many places in the West; we could not make money, because our margin of profit on small branches is very narrow, and being cut narrower every day by the action of provincial governments in introducing iniquitous legislation granting exemptions. I think they are realizing that now and that some of this iniquitous legislation is be ng repealed. I know of cases where first mortgages held by companies in the East have been wiped out by some of that iniquitous legislation. Again the governments are going into competition with us in opening banks. They pay a higher rate for deposits than we do. Well, we cannot do business if the provincial governments take our deposits. We either have to let them go or pay a higher rate.
In another portion of his testimony he gave reasons as to why the cost of doing business was higher in the western provinces than in the East. It is very easy to say that the West is over banked and that a great many of the existing institutions in that part of the country should be closed. But that was not the story ten or fifteen years ago and I do not know how you could very well

eliminate those banks; it could not be done very well by process of law. I have no doubt that many of the banking agencies in the West will be closed particularly in Alberta, and possibly in Saskatchewan, from now on. I doubt very much, however, whether that will be satisfactory to the people of the West. Let me say again that it is not a correct statement of the condition of affairs to say that there is no competition among the banks. The competition is not determined by the question as to whether or not the rate is uniform throughout a large area, or whether it is the same throughout a very large country at a given time. I should think it would be a quite serious matter for many sections of western Canada if these banking agencies were closed. They perform a public service . and are of great convenience to the communities which they serve. I for one, at any rate, am not going to assume the responsibility of altering the section. I think we should consider very carefully the wisdom of changing the section to fix a rate of interest at 7 per cent. That would be a very unwise course to adopt, and I trust the committee will decide that it is not advisable to accept the amendment.
Is the hon. member prepared to wipe out the section altogether?

I am not speaking for the government. So far as I am concerned I think it would be a good way to have the law in reference to interest, but I fear it would meet with opposition from hon. members from the western provinces and I should not like to take the responsibility of saying it should be done.
I do not think that hon. members in this part of the House can be accused of monopolizing the discussion of the bill now before the committee.
Hear, hear.

I am glad that the culprits concede that much. This is an exceedingly important section and to my mind it is an economic absurdity to provide in the Bank Act anything that purports to fix the rate of interest when it does not fix it. That is more than foolish. This question was thoroughly, considered in the committee when arguments pro and con were advanced, and the committee finally disposed of it by making some additions with respect to the question of discounts. As a matter of fact, I submit, it is impossible to fix the rate of interest on money or capital which is invested in a bank or used by a bank for advances to the com-

Bank Act
munity, if you leave unlimited or unrestricted the rates of interest on all other forms of capital invested throughout the entire world. Money as it is represented in capital or in bonds and credit instruments, in bills or exchange and acceptances, is nothing more or less than a commodity, and in every money market in the world this commodity is given for exchange. It is bargained for, it is sold and purchased, and the rate of interest is adjusted accordingly. So that if, according to the arguments of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw), the rate of interest in connection with money in the banks were fixed at seven per cent, there would be no reason for the shareholders or other people to retain their money in that form of investment.	After all we must consider the
question from the point of view of the general public and not of any particular section, and if the rate were fixed at seven per cent, then the shareholders might as well invest their money in any other form or take it to foreign countries where the rate of interest would be higher. I cannot conceive how any hon. member can argue for a moment in support of such a theory.

Will the hon. member
mention one of the countries where the interest is higher?

It may be higher at times in the western states. Money is, in fact, something that is essentially international. When rates are attractive here, it flows across from the States to this side. When they are attractive on the other side, the money flows there. Likewise it may go to Europe, and the credit facilities of banking institutions will deliver money or money credit in almost any part of the world. Nothing is more capable of distribution in small and great quantities than money.
There is no doubt that portions of the western provinces have a grievance as regards interest rates. We saw produced in the committee that considered this question promissory notes bearing 10 to 12 per cent rates of interest, mainly because they were from remote districts. Some hon. members opposite say that there is substantially keen competition in the banking world. I think that is so. That is the case in some towns in the WTest. I know in the little town of Ladner, British Columbia, there are the Royal Bank, the Bank of Commerce and the Bank of Montreal, and I have it on the best of authority that only one of those banks is actually paying, but the competition to get business is keen in the extreme. The presence of so many branch banks has largely brought
that about. I noticed the other day that, in 1890, we had 38 principal banks making returns to the government, with a total capital of some $60,000,000, and we had 402 branch banks. In 1900, we had 36 principal banks with a total capital of $67,000,000, and the number of branch banks had increased to 663. In 1910, we had 33 principal banks, with a total capital of $100,000,000 and the number of branches had increased to 2,368. In 1923, we have the number of principal banks reduced to 17, with a total capital of $125,000,000, but the number of branches has grown in the last thirteen years to 4,472. Every banker knows that these branches do not all pay. There is competition, but there is also the expense of maintaining those branches.
My main purpose in rising at this juncture of this question is to suggest to the members of the committee that the way to remedy the question of the rate of interest is not by non-economic principles, nor by legislation, but by the ordinary methods of demand and supply. I suggest to the committee that the remedying of this question will not take place in Canada, just as the remedying of a number of other questions cannot take place until we have in this country a federal reserve bank system. In the United States, Great Britain and, in fact, Spain and Italy, in all the principal commercial countries of the world, the federal reserve bank system is in existence. This is a centralized system. A bank of rediscount, in its practical operations in the United States, handles the question of high or unfair rates of interest in remote portions of the country by the system of open market operations. Let us say that in the remote district of Calgary, say ao out-of-the-way place, the rate of interest is 25 per cent, and it is necessary to correct that situation. Under the open market operations such as we have in a federal reserve bank system, the board of the federal reserve bank, which has an obligation to the government, to the people at large, as well as an obligation to the banks and other financial institutions, immediately takes steps to place its own money in that area in competition with the money of the ordinary banks, in order to force the rate of interest down. Let us say, in order to carry out the illustrations of the 25 per cent rate of interest in Calgary, that a federal reserve bank through its board would first notify the banks that were charging those excessive rates that the rates .were too high. If the banks did not see fit to correct those rates, the federal reserve board would take its own money, and through the agency
Bank Act

which it has established in Calgary, it would go into that city and say to the people: "You can come to us and borrow money for 6 per cent." How long are any other banks going to lend money for 25 per cent, 10 per cent, or 8 per cent, when a competing institution will lend money at 6 per cent? In other words a federal reserve banking institution will correct an injustice of that kind by the ordinary, sound, economic principle of supply and demand just as it will assist the industrial and commercial community at large in times of stress through facilities of rediscounting paper, and just as in times of elasticity it will correct an undue increase or boom by utilizing the money rates to raise the rates of discount. I wish to lay before the committee the advantages of a federal reserve bank so far as it pertains to and is able to remedy such a question as rates of interest. The Chairman has properly ruled that the discussion must be confined strictly to the clause under consideration, and I hope I have followed his ruling in my remarks.

I wish to make just a few remarks to voice my objection to subclause 1 of section 91 as it stands in this bill. I notice there has been an addition to subclause 1, which is really a beneficial addition. It reads:
The rate of interest or discount charged by the bank shall appear on the face of the note.
That is one amendment that we were able to get through the committee. Out of the many amendments proposed, 10 p.m. that was one of the very few that received favourable consideration. I am quite aware that this matter of interest rates was debated at great length in the committee, and of course we did not accomplish anything in regard to setting a maximum rate. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) stated in his remarks that the interest rate in the West is a practical question. He uttered a truism when he made that statement. It is a practical question. People in the West run up against real, hard, practical facts in the matter of interest rates, and it is not only those who are in financial difficulties who have to pay high and what we might call exorbitant rates of interest. A rural municipality in western Canada with assets of between three and four million dollars must pay 7 per cent, or 7i per cent, or possibly 8 per cent interest. I think Mr. Powell, manager of the Weyburn Security-Bank stated that they charged 8 per cent interest to rural municipalities. No person will discount the * security offered by a rural municipality, and yet the rate charged by the

Weyburn Security Bank is 8 per cent. In our western country an agriculturist must be in exceptionally good circumstances to get money at 8 per cent. The majority pay 9 per cent and a large number pay 10 per cent interest on the money they borrow. If the banks were paying out a correspondingly high rate of interest for the use of the deposits made with them, possibly there would not be the same objection to the high rate which they charge on loans, but we find they pay but 3 per cent for the large bulk of the money that they loan out at 7, 8, 9, or 10 per cent.
I might here make an observation in regard to the Weyburn Security Bank. The hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) stated that if the interest rate were set at 7 per cent this bank would go out of business. Well, it is only fair to say that they pay 4 per cent on deposits; therefore a 7 per cent maximum rate would militate against this bank.
We find that the banks control something over two billion dollars of the people's money, for the use of which they pay 3 per cent. In our western country at least the banks turn that money over at a spread of 5 or 6 per cent and possibly more. Now, it has been argued in the special committee-I do not know to what effect-that if the banks were limited to 7 per cent they would go out of business. I do not believe it, Mr. Chairman; but I do believe that if they were limited to 7 per cent they would curtail some unnecessary expenses. In the town of Weyburn, Saskatchewan, with a population of 3,500 we have seven banks. That is altogether unnecessary. Two banks could handle the business there. In the small town of High River, Alberta, with a population of 1,200, we have five banks- another unnecessary expense. And I need not remind you, Mr. Chairman, that the banks do not do business in shacks or in the same class of buildings that the majority of agriculturists have to live in from whom the banks make their profit. I hope that is quite clear.
Now, it may be asked, have we any proof whether the banks could continue in business if the rate were set at a maximum of 7 per cent.

Before my hon. friend
leaves that part of his remarks dealing with Weyburn, would he tell me how it is that the Weyburn Security Bank, which pays 4 per cent interest on deposits, or 1 per cent higher than any of the other banks pay, has not attracted the deposits which go into the other six banks, if there is no such thing as competition in the banking business?

I think the Weyburn Security Bank did get a large amount

Bank Act
of western money before they opened up a banking business, that is, when they carried on a mortgage business. At that time they paid 4 per cent on deposits. When they launched into the banking business they continued to pay the same rate of interest. Whether they will be able to continue to do so in competition with the other banks I am not prepared to say.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the spread between what the banks pay on deposits and what they realize on loans is to my mind exorbitant. I do not know whether it would be wise to set the maximum at 7 per cent throughout Canada, for the reason that in western Canada possibly the risks during the past years have been greater than in eastern Canada on account of crop conditions. But according to reports from the West at the present time, risks out there will be fewer in the future possibly than they have been in eastern Canada.
Looking across the Pacific to the island-continent of Australia, we have what to my mind is an ideal system for controlling bank rates of interest. There they have established a government banking system known as the Australian Commonwealth Bank. I stated in the special committee that the bank started without capital and has not issued any since. The statement was challenged and it was asserted that the bank did raise or levy a certain amount of capital. In the absence of any further information I am not prepared to admit or refute the statement. But the information I had was that the bank commenced business on deposits taken from the post office and from the people, and has been able to carry on business for ten years by paying from 3 to 4 per cent on deposits and charging a maximum of 6 per cent on loans. And in the decade it has made a profit of something over $18,000,000. Now, it seems to me that if we are not going to be able to set a maximum rate of interest in the Bank Act, we shall have to resort to other ways and means to regulate the bank rate, and I think one good way to effect this regulation is to set up a competitive system that will operate alongside of our present banking system, and so control its rates.
I assume my hon. friend was in the West about 1900. Was there any fall in the average interest rate, say, between 1900 and 1914?

I am prepared to admit that when crops and prices are good and the people in general prosperous, interest lates are low; but when we run up against adverse conditions, as we have for the past
few years, interest rates are high. That is, our financial institutions unduly penalize the country at a time when it is suffering from depression. They should not be permitted to do this.
I would be quite prepared to vote for the amendment, but I am not optimistic enough to hope that the committee is likely to accept it. It seems to me that we are just talking here for the sake of putting forth what we think, and that we hope to attain nothing in the way of any very drastic relief from our present banking system.
Does the hon. member really mean that?
Yes, I do.

Mr. Chairman, not having been a member of the Banking committee I have taken very little part in the discussion, nor do I intend to, but I want to make a few observations on interest rates-a subject that appeals to me very strongly. I notice that in the discussion remarks are frequently made to the effect that this committee sympathises with the difficulties the West is passing through at the present time and would like to give some relief. But unfortunately that sympathy seems to fall short of reaching the point where it might bring relief. In fact, it is rather a passive sympathy. I have listened to the discussion with a great deal of interest, and I may say at the outset that I believe we have a good banking system. Indeed, I am not in favour of upsetting those institutions which have served us well in the past and have weathered the years of trial successfully, without feeling absolutely certain that we have something better to put in their place. For myself, I am willing to go to the extent of supporting only those amendments to the Bank Act that would seem to be almost beyond doubt a benefit. With regard to the high rate charged in the West -the hon, senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) referred to that-I would point out that during the years when we had cheap land, virgin soil which could be conveniently and cheaply cultivated; when weeds were entirely absent and when the farmers, owing to the increase in the value of their land, were growing fairly wealthy without the crop-in those days it was quite natural that the banks and other institutions should charge high rates in the West, because the trade would stand it; and having secured these higher rates they are now very reluctant to give them up. I have thought this matter over carefully, and I have failed to see why in the West, where the security is certain-
Bank Act

in many cases being victory bonds; in many cases wealthy men borrowing small amounts -where, in fact the security was almost as good as the bank itself and the losses of the banks in interest were nil-I have failed to see why a bank in the West doing a good business could not profitably lend money at 7 per cent as they are doing in the East.
Let me make a comparison. Walking the streets of Ottawa I was struck by the great number of bank branches that we have here. One sees a branch of the Bank of Montreal on one corner; he walks a few blocks and sees another branch of the same bank, and so it is with the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Union Bank and others. If it is possible, at the rates of and 7 per cent charged here, for the banks to keep up so many branches within a few blocks of each other, built on land for which a very high price is paid, carried on at great expense, it seems to me that in the comparatively small institutions maintained in western Canada, where there is no loss year after year and where even over a considerable period of years the aggregate loss would be very slight-it seems to me that in those districts the banks could be made to pay at the same rate of interest charged in the East. I believe it is true that in many cases, as the bankers say, they have lost money in the West. Why is that so? They loaned too freely in the arid districts, where the risk was great. They made the same mistake in lending too freely that the farmer made, in many cases, of borrowing too freely. But there is just this difference: in the case of the banks they are assured against loss resulting from their bad judgment, resulting from their lending money where they should not have loaned it.
It was argued in the Banking committee and it has been argued in this committee-if it was not specifically stated, it was implied- that because of these losses the banks in the West should be allowed to charge higher rates of interest. In other words, those who are paying their debts are penalized in order to ensure the banks against the results of their bad judgment. The farmer who made the mistake of borrowing too much must carry his own burden, and he is asked also to carry the burden of the banks where they have used poor judgment in the lending of money. I am inclined to think that what Mr. Powell and others have said is partly true-that if the rates in the West were reduced to 7 per cent the banks would quit business. I say that is partly true. They would quit business in towns where there are twice as many banks as there should be; they would quit business in arid districts 
where the crop fails four and five years in succession. I would be sorry to see the people in those districts subjected to any hardship, but in some parts of the country it does seem to me there is necessity for a clean-up in this connection. The banks and the government cannot continue forever to carry the people in an arid district, and I see no reason why those who live in districts that are not arid should, because of the conditions in the arid districts, be penalized so far as the rate of interest is concerned. I think it is unfair and unjust.
Reference has been made to the charge of two-thirds of one per cent imposed after taxes become due. Let me point out that that is not a rate of interest; that is a penalty which is imposed in order to induce people to pay their taxes when they are due. In fact, in our own municipality higher than two-thirds of one per cent per month is charged; the rate is one per cent per month, yet we have not looked upon it as a rate of interest and it cannot fairly be so considered.
It has been suggested that the law of supply and demand should regulate the interest charge* and the hon. senior member for Halifax has pointed to the fact that so far as deposits are concerned there was competition in Weyburn, for instance, in the matter of interest rates. But that competition affects very few people; it gives no relief. It is the interest on money loaned that is the important thing. It is true that there is a great deal of competition in an effort to get the business, but that competition does not reach the rate of interest on borrowed money. The rate of interest charged by two or three banks in the same town will be exactly the same-that is, the rate they will charge for money loaned, What good would it do if in a town forty or fifty miles away from where the borrower lives some of the banks were charging a lower rate of interest? What relief rvould that give? I cannot go fifty miles away, present my credentials at a bank in that place, and borrow money. They would say, "Why do you not borrow at home?" The only bank from which I can borrow money is the bank that is close to me that knows my financial standing, that keeps track of my business.
It has been stated by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Ladner) that it is impossible, ridiculous-I think he used the word "absurd"-to think of controlling the rates of interest charged by the banks while you allow money lent by other institutions -I suppose he meant mortgage companies and other institutions of that character-to go untrammeled and uncontrolled. I admit that I have a doubt whether a reduction to

Bank Act
a rate of 7 per cent in the West might not be too great a cut, but I believe that a move in that direction might well be made. It is just possible that if the banks lent money at a lower rate of interest their competition would compel the loan companies and the private lenders also to lower their rates. Is it not just as reasonable to expect that that will be the effect as that such a change is impracticable? Is it not quite as reasonable to believe that the other concerns will be compelled to come to the 7 or 7^ per cent rate in order to meet the competition as to believe that it is impossible to control the rate of interest charged by the banks while no control is exercised over the rate charged by other institutions? Very few changes have been made in the Bank Act-I am sorry that more were not made-but I think the committee would be well advised to take this suggestion into their serious consideration. If it is thought that a reduction to 7 per cent is too great a cut, at least it could be made For my part, if it comes to a vote I would take the risk of voting for the 7 per cent. I know the conditions pretty well in the West, and I feel that while the banks would have . to make some readjustments, while they would cease business in certain places and a little hardship might be caused, the change might not be such as to compel them to withdraw from business. I have no doubt that for the most part they would continue as they are, and I am sure that the benefit would very much more than compensate for the loss. It is difficult to get any great reform without some little loss, but I say that in this case the benefits would undoubtedly more than outweigh the loss.
There is a general tendency towards monopoly, and a general tendency so far as the government goes to control monopoly. Recently we had a report handed in by the commission that investigated the Great Lakes freight rates, and one of their recommendations was that a maximum price be set for the carrying of grain upon the Great Lakes. We have never done that in the past. They have in the United States in a partial way, but we have not in Canada. That is a step forward that we have not yet accepted, but I have not very much doubt that when that matter comes before this committee we shall take that step forward in regard to the rates on the Great Lakes, and I believe it will be a wise step. When we control the rates on the railways, and we are going further in that direction every day of necessity because we must do so to protect ourselves, why is it such a disastrous thing to take such a step
in connection with our banks? Surely when we consider the accumulation of money in so few hands we must realize that our banks are becoming more and more monopolistic every day. I hope the committee will look upon this amendment quite seriously. While the Banking committee have thought, I be-live, that too many theories have been presented before it and perhaps have been a little frightened lest too drastic changes should be made, I feel that perhaps the tendency will be to close the door too tight and prevent such reforms as would be in the interest of Canada as a whole. We all know that there have been strong objections to reforms from time immemorial, and it sometimes takes considerable discussion and a lot of educational work before the country can be brought to that stage where they are willing to try something new. As I have said before I am not sure that the risk is too great, and if it comes to a vote I shall vote for the amendment.

I do not wish to prolong
this debate unnecessarily. I know this committee is tired and that perhaps this particular phase of the discussion has been carried on too long already, but this subject is one that particularly appeals to me from a practical standpoint. I do not look at it from a theoretical standpoint at all. I have in view when I consider this question of the interest rate, the practical needs of this country and its condition at the present day and hour.
I must confess, Mr. Chairman, to a very keen sense of disappointment in some ways [DOT] over the outcome of the revision of this act and the form in which it has come before parliament at this time. I was in hopes when the act was referred to the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce, of which I was a member, when it was fully considered there, when all the conditions prevailing throughout this country were laid bare so fully and completely, and when it was reported back to this House that we would have had something more in the way of a detailed statement either from my hon. friend the Minister of Finance or from the chairman of the Banking committee setting forth in brief at least what had been covered in the investigations of that committee, what they had found as to the conditions of the country, together with some concrete suggestions as to how they were going to meet the situation in the West. I felt all through that hearing that these gentlemen had a large sympathy with and interest in the people of the West under prevailing conditions, and I repeat, I am somewhat disappointed that
Bank Act

they did not go into that phase of the question and have some suggestions to make when this act was reported back to this House.
In regard to this interest clause, I am heartily in sympathy with the amendment submitted by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw). I do not believe that this country in any part of it is in a condition to-day to pay a higher rate of interest than seven per cent. I know that in my part of the West we have piled up in the banks thousands upon thousands of dollars in notes and securities of farmers which are bearing very high rates of interest, eight, nine and ten per cent, and if those notes in the hands of the banks continue to accumulate at the rates of interest they are now bearing I do not see how our farmers are going to lift the load and get on their feet.
