The only practical thing that can be done by this act to help them is to reduce the interest rate, and even that will help to only a limited extent, but to my mind, Mr. Chairman, it is the one essential thing. It will open the road, it will implant a feeling of hope and confidence in the minds of the fanners of the West, and if there is anything that is needed above that in this country I hardly know how to express it.
The hon. Minister of Finance said to-day that we had in prospect a very good crop in the West. The reports to that effect I think are true. I have had similar reports, and of course a good crop will have some effect upon the situation, but I cannot see how it can carry us to any very great extent to-* wards the liquidation of the debts that are upon that country. My feeling after carefully canvassing the matter is that not only one good crop will be needed to even help move that load, but seven or eight or nine or ten good crops will be required to accomplish the object which he is hopeful we shall attain. I wish I could be as hopeful of the situation as he is, and I am a man of hope myself. I appreciate the fact that he feels even a little encouragement over the present situation. But suppose this rate is reduced to seven per cent? Is the disaster to the banking institutions of this country that has been apprehended going to occur? I do not believe it.
I believe on the other hand it will result in good to the banks.
I believe that the banks need to have faith and confidence in our great West to a greater extent to-day than even the farmers. I came from the state of Illinois. In that state, from the days of my birth, they have had a maximum rate of interest of 7 per cent. Did that rate of interest ever injure the state of Illinois? Did it ever wreck its banking system, its [Mr. JelliffJ
great commercial institutions or its great factories? But in the last sixty years Illinois has risen from a young state to one of the greatest states in the whole world. Her manufacturing institutions alone turn out each year three billion dollars worth of manufactured goods; more than does the entire Dominion of Canada. Within the last sixty years of the existence of the live stock markets in Chicago over 750 million animals have passed through that market. The Chicago grain market is also one of the great grain markets of the world. Is there any evidence to show that the limitation of the rate of interest to 7 per cent has done any harm there? Can you point to an instance where there has been greater general development, or greater improvement in the welfare of the people?
The same is true of a number of other states. The state of Michigan has had a maximum rate of 7 per cent for a great many years, and it is to-day one of the greatest states in the Union. One of its cities alone has produced a manufacturer who has made greater use of his wealth than possibly any other individual on the American continent to-day. In the state of New York the same beneficial results have been witnessed. There they have had an even lower maximum rate for their general loans, 6 per cent, for many years; and in many other states a low maximum rate of interest has been the rule. Has that low rate of interest ruined those states? Has it injured the state of New York? Do we not go to New York when we want to get the millions that are sometimes necessary to tide us over our own difficulties here? I cannot help but conclude when I look this situation squarely in the face, that neither our banks, nor our financial institutions of any kind, nor any class of our people, have the least reason to fear the fixing of the maximum rate of interest at 7 per cent.
I know what it means to the men out on the farm if we continue the existing rate; if they have to go up against the burden of accumulated indebtedness in our banks at existing rates. It will mean the continual and further crowding down on the perspiring brow of the husbandman of this country a crown of thorns; the man who, by his industry, is producing year after year not only the food for his own family but for the families of those engaged in other occupations, and for the hungry and needy across the seas; the man by whose industry a new stream of golden wealth is produced each year to vitalize and keep up our transportation systems, and to bring strength and prosperity into all the avenues of our commercial and in-

Bank Act
dustrial life. We must take these things into consideration. We must do all we can, when revising this Bank Act, to bring needed relief to our people. They are looking for that relief and they will be disappointed if they do not get it. I picked up and put into my pocket this evening a little volume from which I desire to read a brief extract. It is from the speech which a great American, Abraham Lincoln, whom the world has always loved and admired, made on the subject of slavery -I will merely read this fragment from the speech:
Free labour has the inspiration of hope; pure slavery has no hope. The power of hope upon human exertion and happiness is wonderful. The slave-master h.imself has a conception of it, and hence the system of tasks among slaves. The slave whom you cannot drive with the lash to break seventy-five pounds of hemp in a day, if you will task him to break a hundred, and promise him pay for all he does over, he will break you a hundred and fifty. You have substituted hope for the rod. And yet perhaps it does not occur to you that to the extent of your gain in the case, you have given up the slave system and adopted the free system of labour.
That -is what I believe we should all do at this time in regard to our country if we have in mind its future development. Implant hope and confidence in our people and with it will come prosperity and happiness. Let us do this much in the way of limiting this burden; restrict this interest rate to seven per cent, help the people out of this difficulty, and throw light upon their future pathway. I do hope, Mr. Chairman, this amendment will be accepted.

I do not desire to delay the House at any great length, but I wish to put myself on record as being in favour of the amendment now being considered. We have at present in the Bank Act a clause which pretends to make the maximum rate of interest 7 per cent, but it has never been effective. I think, in view of the evidence that has been adduced this session before different committees of the House, we cannot help but believe that the banks can do business on a 7 per cent rate of interest. Wo have the evidence of different rural credit associations in Canada who are doing business on a spread of one per cent in interest between what their money cost them and the rate at which they loan it, and they are making surpluses on that margin of one pe: cent. At the same time we have banks, or bankers coming before different committees of the House and plainly stating that they cannot do business on a spread of less than 5 and 6 per cent. Now, Mr. Chairman, if the present banking system is as efficient as our leading bankers would lead us to believe,
why is it that they cannot do business as cheaply as amateur organizations, as you might call the rural credit associations of Canada? Because, when these rural credit associations were first started it was said by ihe banks and the bankers that they could not function at that cheap rate of interest, they could not carry on their business on a spread of one per cent, but they have proved conclusively that this is possible.
There is another feature that would look to be in favour of the banks. The turnover of the rural credit associations is slow, it is on long terms; the turnover is once in thirty 3rears. If they can do business on a turnover cf one per cent, it does not look logical to me that the banks cannot do business on a spread of less than 5 and 6 per cent on their turnover, especially when they turn their capital over several times during the year.
As I said, I do not wish to detain the committee, but these are some of the thoughts ihat have occurred to me. It has been said that if the maximum rate of interest is made lew, and the banks are compelled to live up to it, that a good number of the branch banks in the West will cease to do business. Personally, Mr. Chairman, from the information I have, I think it would be a good thing for the country if some of the branch banks did cease to do business in some of the towns, not only in western Canada but m eastern Canada. We have the spectacle of three or four branch banks in a town, surrounded possibly, by a good farming community where there is only about business enough for one branch bank. We thus have two, or three, or four branch banks competing for the business, which means that the people who patronize these banks must pay the overhead expense of four banks when there should only be one. I think the fact that there are too many branch banks is one of the reasons why the banks have been charging a rate of interest that is not justified by actual practice in other lines.
There is another feature which was very well brought out in the committee investigations this session, and that is the fact that agriculturists pay a higher rate of interest than people engaged in any other industry in Canada, and also higher than those in any other country one might mention. Nearly every other country has an extended rural credit scheme whereby the farmer can get cheap capital; and I hope that the government will see fit to institute in the very near future, some form of rural credits financed federally. The report submitted today by the special committee on agriculture
Bank Act

will, I presume, be under discussion later on when I shall have something to say in this connection. I quite realize that anything I might say on the question now would be out of order. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee, but I must go on record as being in favour of the amendment.

I, too, want to go on record on this subject, and I want at the same time to deal with two matters referred to by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). Speaking with regard to a certain economist, that hon. gentleman said that in practice there was such a thing as putting the rate up under certain conditions, while it came down on other occasions. So far as we are concerned, I want to say that we have never known the rate to come down; it has always gone up in the West. Another thing that seemed rather peculiar to me was the fact that while the hon. member would have the banks charge seven per cent, he would also allow them to charge a much greater rate; and we have it on record that the average rate in the case of the Weybum Security Bank is 9 per cent. The hon. member for Halifax quoted the manager of the Weyburn Security Bank and observed that we all considered him honest in his statements. The question is, however, did he submit any facts? Did he produce his books to show that his institution could not continue in business on a seven per cent basis? It was simply a matter of evidence, and before a man makes a statement of that kind he should be able to back it up with facts. This gentleman should have been able to prove that his bank would go out of business under different circumstances. We have it on the authority of western members that many of the farmers are going out of existence because a higher rate than seven per cent is being charged. The senior member for Halifax said that there was competition among the banks. Well, if there is I have not had the pleasure of seeing very much of it. I believe there is competition in the United States because the banks are very easily multiplied there. But it is difficult to multiply the banking institutions in this country. The trouble is that on the contrary, they are reduced in number here until to-day they have a monopoly of the credit situation in Canada.
The hon. member continually referred to the issuance on the part of the banks as money. I do not altogether agree with that. It is a matter of credit;' and Siegel of the United States says, in regard to interest, that the credit of a bank is valuable only when

it can be changed for real money. We have not the gold standard in Canada, and I do not think you could go to an ordinary bank to-day and get real money for the credit they offer you. Yet, notwithstanding that they are privileged to extend credit, they are given the further privilege of monopolizing the interest rate. I for one protest against this; and I say that if the government make regulations in regard to banking in this country they ought to have the same authority in the matter of rates and should be able to stipulate what should be the legal rate for the banks in the West to charge the farmers who borrow money from them.
The hon. member for Halifax also declared that as we became an older country and entered a little more extensively into mixed farming the time would come when we should have a cheaper rate, as in the East. By that time, however, many of us will be under the sod. No; what we want is something that will help us in our present situation. We are not looking so much to the future; we are very much concerned about what' can be done to remedy the evils that exist under present circumstances. Now that there is deflation in the West and conditions are not optimistic, it does seem to me that the present time is most opportune to lower the rate, as suggested; and for that reason I am heartily in support of the proposed amendment. I believe it is quite within the authority of parliament to enact that 7 or 7i per cent shall be the maximum rate legally chargeable by any bank which is given a charter by federal legislation.

The only hon. member on the government side of the House who has spoken against the amendment is the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). It is rather unfortunate that we should find it necessary to bombard one hon. member all the time, but as he has avowed himself the protagonist of the Bank Act and-shall I say?-the apologist of the bankers in this regard, there is nothing left for us but to deal with the arguments he has presented to the committee. In opposing the amendment moved by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) the hon. member for Halifax said that money was much like anything else; and upon that basis he proceeded to build up an argument. Now, as a matter of fact, money is in no respect like anything else, and that is where the hon. member erred. On that false hypothesis he argued that interest could not be fixed because money flows to points where the highest rates are

Bank Act
paid. In other words, he placed money on the basis of ordinary commodities which rise and fall with the demand. If this were absolutely true, money would flow to the highest interest point in such volume as to reduce the rate of interest to the lowest possible minimum. That is what happens in the case of potatoes or in the case of clothing: the commodity flows in such quantities to the place of greatest demand,-which is naturally the place where the highest price is offered-but as the demand is satisfied there ensues a reaction. The price drops, and the commodity must find some other outlet. This is not true in regard to money. In order to refute the theory used as argument one may refer to the hon. member's own statements. He showed that the rate of interest in New York was different from that in Chicago or in the western states of the American union. It is true in Canada that the interest rates are low in the East as compared with the West. If money flowed, as the hon. member says, to the point where interest rates are highest, it should flow in such volume that in western Canada one would find it at reduced rates of interest, in a short time and ultimately at the minimum. But as the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Lewis) has pointed out, we have no experience of any falling of rates in the West. The only thing we know about them is that they are climbing up.
Take the case of Great Britain as compared with Canada. Money is a free trade commodity, and it flows from one country to another declares the hon. member for Halifax. Now this is clearly not true. Interest rates in Great Britain are much lower than they are in Canada. Therefore, if his argument were sound, money ought to flow from Great Britain into Canada just like the Gulf stream going the opposite way, and ultimately we would have as low and even a lower rate of interest at times in Canada than they have in Great Britain. But that is not so. There must be something wrong then with the basis of the hon. gentleman's argument. While he accepted this principle, it seems to me that he departed from it before he finished with his argument, because he said in reply to a question which I put to him in this connection, that this flow did not continue in a volume sufficient to reduce the rate of interest to western Canada because the security was not good. This argument then must be applied to Canada as a whole in relation to Great Britain which is to say that Canadian security is not good enough to attract money from Great Britain. But that this form of
reasoning means that my hon. friend either does not think the rate of interest is the important thing or else that he is confused in his thinking, for he virtually abandons his first contention and says now that the security for money, not the rate of interest, is the important thing. Therefore, it is the security of the investment, more than interest rates, that guides the price level. If that is so, then the whole argument of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) falls to the ground, and it cannot be applied to the present debate.
He also referred to the statement of Professor Gustav Cassel to the effect that price levels are controlled by interest charges. But after accepting this, the hon. member for Halifax proved that securities controlled interest, and therefore securities must control price levels. Therefore, he is not in agreement with Professor Cassel as he declared himself to be; he is in opposition to him. But let me for the moment accept the statement of Professor Cassel, although I have no more reverence for that professor than I have for a hundred others, and simply because he says it, is not a conclusive argument to my mind that it is so. I am prepared to admit, for the sake of argument, that there is something in the statement of the professor, namely, that the rate of interest may have some relation to prices. Even so, it can still continue, for the proposal of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw) fixes only the maximum rate of interest. There is a great range from 7 per cent to 1 per cent; that leaves plenty of room for the affecting of price levels. So even accepting the statement of Professor Cassel as being sound economics, we still may utilize the truth of that after having passed the amendment which has been moved.
I am not prepared to admit that the rate of interest is even an important factor in fixing prices. Let me give you a parallel to this. It used to be believed that profits were regulated by the prices charged for goods, and those who handled goods naturally supposed that the higher the price they charged the more profit they would make. But after a while they found that turnover was more important than high prices; they found that if they could cut their prices just a little above the cost of production and overhead, they could double or redouble their sales, and they could make more money than by charging high prices. That is just as true when you apply it to money, since money is used as a commodity, as it would be in the case of any other commodity in the market. If you cut
Bank Act

the price of money b.y reducing interest charges, you have immediately the effect of increasing the loans, and by increasing the loans that are made, you increase the business that will be done by the banks. There is no loss; in fact, there might be an increase of the interest charges on the whole, and thus the price levels would still be affected in a similar fashion providing of course that interest rates do affect prices.
But the chief point to be considered in this argument is that while the hon. member for Halifax argues strenuously that interest rates cannot be fixed, and I think the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Ladner) said that the proposal was an economic absurdity, yet against all these the fact remains that interest rates are fixed in Canada to-day. They are fixed in Great Britain; they are fixed in New York, according to the statement of the hon. gentleman for Halifax. If they are fixed by the banks, why cannot they be fixed by this government in the interest of the people? If these hon. gentlemen are to be logical in their argument, they must face their own logic. After proving to us in one part of the argument that interest rates could not be fixed at all, they quietly tell us that interest rates are fixed now; that they are the same throughout Great Britain at any one given time; that they are the same in New York; that they are the same in eastern Canada. If they are fixed already by the Bankers' Association of this country, by the financial associations of other countries, they are fixed by them in their own interest.
When I said that the market rates for money were fixed at certain centres, I did not say that they were fixed by bankers or by law. I meant that they were fixed by market conditions.

As a matter of fact, they are not fixed by market conditions, as I have shown to hon. members, because in that case we would have the same rate of interest all over this country, or at least the rates would be at some time lower in the West than in the East, caused by the flow of money to the highest market, but this never happens. The rate of interest in this country is 11 p.m. fixed by the Bankers' Association.
Therefore, the very point that is characterized by an hon. member as an economic absurdity is now in practice in Canada, and the very point which the hon. member for Halifax says would, perhaps, result in the destruction of the banking system, although he did not say that in those terms, is already in practice in Canada. The point is, if the Bankers' Association, having a virtual mono-

poly in this country, has already fixed interest charges both east and west, fixed them on the loans they make, on the deposits they take from the people, fixed them in their interest in order to make profits for the bank, it is highly desirable and practicable that this committee and this parliament should fix the rate of interest so as to take care of the well-being of the people.
Let me say that I would be in favour of no restriction whatsoever if the banks did not have a monopoly. Break up your monopoly, and we do not need any such restrictions. Ordinarily we should have a clean-cut competition in banking, and if that were so interest rates would depend upon the amount of money available for loans. But in a country where there are seventeen banks meeting in one association, fixing interest rates in each community at the same rate in every bank, then as regards interest rates we have a monopoly, and the only possible protection that the people have against such a monopoly is such a restriction as is proposed in the amendment under consideration.

Many hon. gentlemen in this House to our right and on the treasury benches seem to take it for granted that the only problems in western Canada are those of poor crops and they refer repeatedly to the drouth districts in the south and southwest. I live in the northeastern part of Saskatchewan where we always have good crops, where in twenty years we have not had an actual crop failure, where we have abundance of rain, where we have the best of soil -in a word, where nature has indeed been most kind to us. Yet we have problems so acute there that whole districts are being deserted. If you were to ask the average citizen there to-day as to what these problems were, he would in all probability summarize them under four heads: tariff, transportation rates, markets, interest. And if I were asked to put my finger on the most urgent need of the community and on its most vital problem I would say, without a moment's hesitation, interest. Hon. gentlemen who come from the old settled parts of the Dominion perhaps do not appreciate the difficulties in a newly settled country. Your farmers as I know them in the Maritime provinces, and to a lesser extent in Ontario, are in a great many eases either on inherited farms or farms that they paid for years ago, so that the interest problem does not enter into their production costs at all. But in a new country it is generally the poorer classes of men who come to carve out a home in the wilderness, and interest with them is a

Bank Act
very vital problem. Indeed, I think there is nothing that would put western Canada mo-e quickly on the map to-day than a reduction in the rate of interest. Our hon. friends on the government benches and on our right are boosting immigration, and some very hard things have been said against hon. gentlemen in this section of the House because we have pointed out the fallacy of any such policy at the present time. To hon. gentlemen to our right and to hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches I would say that if they are really sincere and want to attract immigrants, if they want to re-establish the farmers of Canada to-day, they can do this in no better way than by assisting us in securing a reduction of interest. The interest paid by the average farmer in the West to-day is crushing out his economic life an! is driving tens of thousands off the land. I am not entirely clear in my own mind whether this question should be dealt with through the Bank Act or under a rural credit scheme. But if nothing can be done here-and I take it for granted that our friends are not seriously considering this amendment-then in all seriousness I say: If you are sincere and want to see people come into the country to help in its development and to share our financial burdens, then by all means assist us to get some form of rural credits that will cut the interest rates which are so burdensome on our western farmers to-day. Tens of thousands of these men are plodding along in such poor financial shape that they can see no possible chance of getting through. The rate of interest every year means to them more perhaps than the whole profit on their crop under the most favourable circumstances. But if some scheme can be devised for the reduction of the interest rate, and their indebtedness spread over a long period of years, I can assure hon. members opposite and on our right that they will no longer hear the bitter complaints from western Canada that they are hearing to-day, for they will have solved one of the greatest problems of the West. To our good protectionists-and I refer to my hon. friends on the treasury benches, because they are just as much protectionists as hon. members to our right-I say if you want to hear less about the tariff from us and to get us to accept it under protest, help us to reduce this interest rate. We will never be favourable to the tariff, but we will be prepared to accept it under protest, as well as a good many other things, for the sake of peace and harmony if you assist us in tins one vital, urgent need of the western country to-day.

Its earnings last year were equivalent to 16.95 per cent on the capital stock, while for the eight-year period from 1915 to 1922 its earnings averaged 18.80 per cent annually. When they want a little banking accommodation in this country and are asked to pay that rate there will be as much dissatisfaction among them as among the Hebrideans whose case we discussed in the House a few days ago.
There is one other thing I would like to mention as a justification for limiting the rate of interest charged by the banks, and that is that they have a very special privilege granted to them in being able to issue notes. That is a privilege which other corporations or private parties who may charge a higher rate of interest do not have and surely we have a right to expect some return from the banks for this very special privilege. The hon. member for Halifax referred to the statement of Mr. Powell of the Weyburn Security Bank that if the rate of interest were limited to 7 per cent they would go out of business. I want to say that a great many farmers in western Canada, I think the majority of them, would come to this House if they had the opportunity and tell hon. members that at the present prices they receive for their products 'and the present cost of production, if they have to pay more than 7 per cent they will go out of business. It may be a case of choosing whether you want banks or whether you want farmers in western Canada. I do not think the banks will produce anything that will furnish traffic for the railroads to enable them to earn the dividends of which we have heard so much, but the farmers, if they are considered in this matter, will produce something for these railroads to haul. I think in this House we should try to be fair to all parties.
The general manager of the Bank of Commerce, Sir John Aird, when he was before the Banking committee when this very subject was under discussion-I think that was the time-gave as one excuse for the high rates of interest which they charged in the West the high cost of doing business there. And one of the reasons which he gave for their high cost of operation was that they had opened branches in western Canada to provide positions for returned men. Now, Mr. Chairman, I want to put this up to the members of the committee very squarely: Is it a fair proposition to place upon the producers in western Canada this task of furnishing positions for returned men? If the

banks want to furnish positions for these returned men, and I think they should, they might do it in some other part of the country that can stand the expense better than western Canada can.
The banks in western Canada are charging this high rate of interest because of the mad rush of the banks there to establish branches. In the year 1919 there were approximately 900 branch banks opened in Canada. Does any hon. member of this committee think that the banks were justified in opening that number of new branches? I have not the figures here, and I am sorry that I have not, showing the increase in population in Canada in that year. I do not think it was very great, and I cannot for the life of me see that there was any good reason for the opening of 900 branches in the Dominion in that year. Why the banks, should attempt to saddle on the people the result of their own-I think I may say-foolish action in this case is more than I can "understand. I maintain, Mr. Chairman, that if the majority of our Canadian banks had been as well managed as they should have been-as well managed for instance as the Bank of Nova Scotia-they would all be able to return a very handsome dividend if the maximum rate of interest they were allowed to charge had been 7 per cent.

in western Canada, I make the statement that there is very little competition among the banks in the matter of interest. There is some competition in service, of course. Possibly we have it straight now. I move in amendment that subsection l of section 91 be struck out and the following Mibstituted therefor:
(1)	The bank may stipulate for, take, reserve, or exact any rate of interest or discount but not exceeding 8 per cent per annum and may receive and take in advance any set rate.
(2)	The rate of interest or discount charged by the bank shall appear on the face of the note, bill or other evidence of debt.
(3)	In the event that a greater rate than 8 per *cent per annum has been paid to the Bank, then the person by whom it has been paid or his legal representative, may recover in any court the excess interest thus paid, provided such action is commenced within two years from the time such excess interest was paid.
(4)	In any suit, action or other proceeding concerning a bank loan wherein it is alleged that the amount [DOT]of interest paid or claimed exceeds the rate of eight per centum per annum, the court may reopen the transaction and take an account between the parties, and may, notwithstanding any statement of settlement of account, or any contract purporting to close previous dealings and create a new obligation, reopen any account already taken between the parties, and relieve the person under obligation to pay from payment of any sum in excess of the legal rate of interest and if any such excess has been paid, or allowed in account, by the debtor, may order the bank to repay it, and may set aside either wholly or in part, or revise, or alter, any security given in respect of the transaction.
The latter part of the amendment is the same as that moved by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Shaw). I hope this amendment will receive the support of the committee. Hopeless.
This question of interest rates is, without doubt, the most vital one facing western Canada to-day. Because of a series of bad years in places, because of low prices for the crops that were raised in other places, because of a general process of deflation involving live stock, grain and other produce of all kinds, because, to a large extent, of the Fordney tariff practically prohibiting the entry of cattle from Canada into the United States, because of the tariff which this country has imposed and which bears heavily upon the people of western Canada, because of the high transportation rates and combines, but especially because of high interest rates, the condition of the farmers of western Canada is reduced to a state of almost insolvency. You find to-day by far the greater majority of the farmers of western Canada carrying great accumulated amounts of debt, upon which they are paying interest rates that have been increasing during the last two years and that are now at a point that the farmers cannot continue to pay them and stay in the farming business. AVhat is the use of filling up that country with immigrants if they cannot live when they come there? We cannot contend that this is not a national question, and it is a sad sight to me to see hon. members opposite dealing with the matter in the most perfunctory manner, disregarding every argument brought to bear on it from this side. It seems utterly useless to endeavour to influence their minds in this matter, and we 
have no hope of being able to. Hon. members have no proposals before the committee for a rural credit scheme, and I venture to say that it is impossible that they will have one at this session. Therefore, there is no hope. We will come back next year-at least some may; we cannot tell what may happen -and there may be another discussion, but we have no guarantee that there will be a discussion of this question.
May I for a moment endeavour to intimate to hon. members who will listen- and some ought to listen-the manner m which loans are taken out in western Canada? A farmer may happen to require a loan in the spring to carry on the year's farming operations. He goes to the bank manager, and he makes out a statement. He states to him every asset he has, the amount of the stock and its value, the amount of the improvements and their value, the amount of his land and its value, and if he does not own it all, his equity in the land, the number of buildings he has and so on. In short he gives him a regular bank statement of all his assets. The bank manager will then say to him: "I will refer this matter to the office at Calgary"-or Saskatoon or Winnipeg, as the case may be-"and I will let you know the result in a week or ten days." At the end of that time the fanner goes in, and if he. is very fortunate, the manager extends the loan at a rate of eight per cent. That is the general procedure until, as I say, recent years. With the rate of eight per cent the farmer is about to leave satisfied, but on reading the note he discovers that it is made out for three months and he tells the manager that he cannot pay it in three months; that that will be in the midst of his summer operations, *and he will have nothing to sell at that time of the year. The reply is that that is a mere formality, and that the farmer can come in at the end of the three months and renew the note. At the end of three months the farmer goes back to have that note renewed, and the bank manager generally informs him that unfortunately, conditions are not as good as they were when he issued the note, or he gives some other excuse. He may say that money is tightening. He has got to call in the loan. If the farmer cannot pay now he is told, "Well, we will renew the loan all right, but you will have to give us additional security and perhaps an increased rate of interest or both." However, it has not been the general practice of the banks to increase the rate of interest until the end of the year. At that time, if it has been impossible for the farmer to pay his full indebtedness-and I may say that owing to present conditions

Bank Act
there have been very few who have been able to pay their debts in full in western Canada-the procedure is to increase the rate of interest and, whenever possible, obtain all additional security.
The banks go further. If the farmer has any liquid assets, such as live stock, then, disregarding entirely market conditions, he is absolutely obliged to put them up for sale. My constituency is about 12,000 square miles in area and is situated in the most densely populated portion of Alberta. My hon. friend from Battle River (Mr. Spencer) represents a constituency which runs into the north country and is entirely a mixed farming district. The southern half of my constituency happens to be devoted to grain growing entirely, but the northern portion is like that of my friend from Battle River a mixed farming district. We sent out a questionnaire to our constituents some time ago, and the answers we received indicate that wherever stock-raising was engaged in a few years ago the banks encouraged the farmers to purchase more stock. I can give the committee my own practical experience in this respect. I happened to attend a stock sale at the Pat Burns Imperial ranch at Rumsey a few years ago and the manager of the local bank was also present. As a matter of fact he was sitting on the top rail of the corral beside me. I happened to have plenty of feed that year and I said to him, "Do you think this stock would be a safe investment?" He said, "You cannot make any mistake in such an investment." I asked him, "Will you advance me the necessary money to purchase some of this stock if you think it is all right?" "Certainly," he said, "you can have as much credit as is necessary to stock your farm." I accepted the offer and was encouraged to purchase stock at $75 to $85 a head. I admit that I should not have been so foolish, but I took it for granted that the bank manager knew conditions, and so I followed his advice. That kind of advice has been followed unfortunately by all too many farmers in western Canada. Credit has also been urged upon them by a system of propaganda something like this:	Do not put
all your eggs into one basket-go in for mixed farming-if you want to go in for hogs come and see your branch manager-if you want to go in for cattle come and see your branch manager-we advise you to go into dairying, see your bank manager. We were encouraged, we went to see our bank manager, and as a result we invested in these things-many of us to our great regret. After having held that live stock for two or three years the market, as you know, fell to pieces when the Fordney tariff was put into effect. But no mercy was
shown by the banks. Our stock was there, our productive capacity was there, but owing to causes over which we had no control the price of cattle broke badly. Did the banks of western Canada help the farmers to tide over that period? Did they say to us, "We will not press you, we will help you to carry on until conditions improve and you can find a market for your stock?" I mentioned to one bank manager the possibility of the removal of the British embargo on cattle. He laughed at me and said, "That is simply a political football; it will never be removed." And the farmers were forced to sell their cattle. I use the word "forced" advisedly. A farmer who had a poor crop and could get little or nothing for it was compelled to sell his other liquid assets to meet his bank loan. In many cases after such forced sales the farmers still owed money to the banks. Many of these farmers had to give additional mortgages at 9 per cent. At the present time I am paying 9 per cent on a ten-year mortgage.
We cannot any longer pay that rate either to the mortgage companies or to the banks, and if this committee does not take some steps to restrict the profiteering banks I cannot without hesitation tell hon. members what will happen. Certainly I hate to think of the future condition of western Canada. After all, this is a national question. Our prosperity out there will influence conditions in the East. If we ever get out of this morass of debt, not only will the country generally be improved immensely through productive development by hopeful farmers, but this prosperity will have a reflex effect on the business of eastern Canda. If hon. members will discuss the present situation with any business men in this city, they will be answered as I was answered the other day. I asked one business man what he thought were the prospects for the fall trade, and he replied, "They do not look good." But I said, "We are going to have a good crop in western Canada this year." He said, "Yes, but I am afraid you cannot pay your debts." And it was only too true.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I wish to place on record one or two examples, not at great length, of the oppressive character of banking practice in western Canada. This is a letter concluding answers to the questionnaire received from Mr. C- A. Wynn of Carmangay, Alberta, and is typical. He writes:
This particular district was settled up by people from eastern Canada and the States some eighteen years ago. They have built up comfortable homes here only to find themselves faced with the situation where it will take practically all their crop to pay the interest on their loans. So for this reason quite a num-
Bank Act

ber are contemplating leaving the country almost at once, crop or no crop, unless there is some relief in sight.
Here are a few of the questions set out on the questionnaire with the answers received :
14.	Has your bank requested payment of their clients' liabilities in full with the promise of extension of credit?
A. Yes.
15.	Has your bank ever broken its promise to reissue credit as per previous question?
A. Yes.
16.	If so, in about what percentage of cases?
A. Could not say definitely, but perhaps 25 per cent.
1 think, Mr. Chairman, that those bankers who may read some part of these proceedings would be well advised to take to heart this admonition: Do not encourage or permit local branch managers to urge a farmer to liquidate a debt regardless of cost at the end of the year on the promise of a renewal of credit for the coming years' operations unless the bank is willing to extend the line of credit. Only too many cases have arisen where the banker has encouraged liquidation at all costs and promised a renewal of credit, but has afterward broken his pledge. That is not going to improve conditions in western Canada, nor is it going to increase the confidence of our farmers in the banking system.
Touching briefly on the answers to the questionnaire I sent out, I would say that the term of a note to the farmer in western Canada is three months. Hon. members can well undestand that that is altogether too short. The interest charge in all districts is never lower than 8 per cent, and in most of the 12,000 square miles-and my hon. friend from Battle River has exactly similar answers covering another 12,000 square miles corroborating in every degree the answers I have received from the southern part of the province-it is 8 per cent compounded, or over. Now, that situation cannot continue. In by far the great majority of cases, all notes are discounted, at time of issue. But it is not a constant practice; there are a few cases reported where a farmer, observing that the hanker is discounting the note at the time of issue protests so vigorously that the banker has been known not to insist on the discount. But too few farmers have the courage to insist, and I do not know whether they would be successful if they insisted as a whole.
Every one of these reports-and I have roughly one hundred of them-indicates that it is impossible under present conditions in western Canada to carry on at 8 per cent or over. A large number of these reports deal with caveats filed by the bank against grain, f.Mr. E. J. Garland.]
so that as soon as a farmer has hauled his grain to the elevator the elevator company makes the cash ticket out to the bank instead of to the farmer. I do not know whether in most of these oases there was collusion with the elevator companies, but I had a letter from Mr. H. W. Leonard, secretary of the Constituency Association at Tudor, Alberta, near Rockyford, in which he stated that an attempt had been made by the bank manager there-I believe it was the Bank of Commerce-to get the elevators to act as collectors for the banks last year at harvest time when the grain was coming in; but fortunately the elevators refused to act. The depletion of the population due to the condition out there is so appalling that I hesitate to give the facts to the committee. But reverting for a moment to the question of interest rates, may I say that in respect to those 12,000 square miles I have received reports from twenty-seven large districts in which the interest is 8 per cent compounded, 9 per cent, 10 per cent, and, in some eases 12 per cent. For example, in the district ol Morrin notes are issued compounded every three months at 8 per cent. In the district of Craigmyle, the rate is 9 per cent, Royal Bank; Big Valley, 9 per cent, Royal Bank and Imperial Bank; Delia, 9 per cent, Bank of Montreal and Bank of Commerce; Hanna, from 8 to 10 per cent and in some cases 12 per cent, Bank of Toronto, Bank of Commerce, Union Bank. In the district of Pa'T the average is 9 per cenh-and by the way, in case a question may be asked me, I would inform the hon. senior member for Halifax that these are averages; they are not isolated instances. The average at Parr is 9 per cent; that is the average for the whole district. At Richdale, it is 10 per cent, Bank of Toronto; at Gleichen, 8 per cent, Bank of Commerce and Royal Bank; at Sunnynook, 8 per cent, Union Bank and Bank of Toronto; at Pandora, 9 per cent, Bank of Toronto; Lonebutte, 9 per cent, Union Bank and Bank of Commerce; Carolside, 9 per cent, Union Bank and Bank of Toronto; Cessford, 10 per cent, Bank of Toronto; Clivale, 8 and 9 per cent, Bank of Commerce and Union Bank; Halb'-day, 9 per cent, Union Bank; Carmangay, 8 per cent, Bank of Commerce; Vulcan, 9 per cent, Bank of Hamilton, and so on. That will give hon. members a fairly accurate idea of the situation there and the rates of interest we have been charged. The hon. senior member for Halifax refers to the costs of operating branch banks, of the expansion of operations of the banks, as one of the causes for the higher rates of interest in the West.

Bank Act
May I remind him in that connection that efforts were made in the committee on Banking and Commerce to recall the bankers in order to ask them specifically for that information. We had no evidence before the committee on Banking and Commerce that would justify the hon. member for Halifax in making that statement-not one tittle of evidence to that effect was adduced. We had simply the bald statements of two bankers, but no evidence. We made an effort to secure that evidence, but the request was refused by the committee; we who asked for it were voted down.
I need not deal further with the question of competition; it has been gone into ver. fully by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote). But I would like to touch on the other aspect of the western Canadian banking conditions that have led to high interest rates, and ask the question, is it our fault, or is it the banks' fault? I wish to quote from page 88 of a book bj' Mr. William Long Baker entitled "Money Monopoly vs. the Community Dollar." Mr. Baker was formerly supervisor of branches for the Standard Bank of Canada, but he left that position to endeavour to form and secure a charter for a commonwealth bank in this country. He says:
It was remarked at the beginning of the preceding chapter that while the banks act in concert in matters furthering their own interests, such as interest rate, legislation and all subjects and phases likely to culminate in organized opposition, yet they are engaged with one another in a struggle for supremacy in business and we have seen a contest between two banks for leading place as Canada's greatest bank. Every bank is trying to show larger totals, larger business than its class competitor. This has led to one of the most insane practices imaginable, that of opening branches where they are not required.
Now, that is only too true, I will not delay the committee in going into the aspect of the question, Mr. Chairman, but you have heard the statements of hon. members around me. The hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) dealt with that point; he mentioned High River as an example, as well as some other towns. I could mention dozens of places where two or more banks are operating but where there is not business enough for one. I quote further from Mr. Baker's work:
It seems hardly possible that men who preach economy, efficiency and avoidance of unnecessary expansion-
And that is the advice we have from bankers.
-would themselves practise the very reverse. Two banks have been known to open their offices in a village on the same day, in fact this may be said to be a common occurrence. Bank A and Bank B may
each have a branch at X. A few miles away is a small fanning locality where Bank A has deposits of $100,000 lodged at their X office. Bank B conceives the idea of opening a branch at the smaller locality and Bank A jumps in immediately to protect its business. There is not enough business to warrant one branch but the fight for business, no, for deposits, goes on, at the expense of the public, and at the expense of derks who eke out a bare existence on half pay. An analysis of Canada's branches made some time ago, showed the following:

I wish to support that statement.
Five hundred and fifteen offices at two-branch points-
" Two-branch points "-points where there are two branch banks.
-could be closed, as there are no towns with only two banks where one could not do the work. It is not necessary to deal with each class, but anyone may estimate that 1,600 branches could be closed releasing probably $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 of capital- and making an annual saving of $12,000,000. This would be allowing an average of less than $8,000 for salaries of manager and staff, rents and all incidental expenses. Additional staff might be required at many points to handle the increased business and there would naturally be some additional expense, but in the majority of cases it would be found that no extra staff would be required. Think of it! Wasting, we shall say, eight or ten million dollars each year in a race for supremacy, in a mad scramble for deposits while bank clerks live or try to live on starvation salaries.
That alone is not the whole story. Not only did they expand into these places where they are not needed, not only did they double and treble the number of branches at places where the business would justify but one, but they built as one hon. gentleman has said, the most expensive buildings in the town. They
Bank Act

fitted them with the most expensive furnishings, and filled them with the most luxurious flowers and ferns and creeping plants so that you enter a most gorgeous palace when you go into the bank, hat in hand, and go down on your knees to borrow money. When I came a homesteader to my present town nearly eighteen years ago, there was no bank, but there came to it two years later an assistant bank manager from a town in that district. He came up by train twice a week to a little shack about twelve by sixteen with a counter in it, and he performed all the functions of a bank in that district admirably. But that was not good enough. Just as soon as the bank could get around to it a contract for a store-shaped building was made and a large frame structure secured. Into it were placed most expensive fittings, with elaborate counters, swivel chairs and costly furniture of all kinds. But still that was not enough. Within eighteen years they had jumped from a shack to a one-storey frame shack, to a two-storey frame building with solid oak partitions *jetween the offices and the outer public hall and with a specially built floor, and as I said, the inside was festooned with green creeping things in order to harmonize with the green things that came in there to borrow money.
That is not an isolated case by any means, Mr. Chairman. It is a common everyday sight in the West. Sixteen miles to the south of that town there are two large banks, one of them a large two-storey brick building and the other an expensively-built frame building. One of these banks of half the size could accommodate all the business that is to be done in that town, but there you have two immense banks with all these expensive fittings. That is one of the reasons possibly why the rate of interest is so high. The other reason may be because it is necessary to pay the large and persistent dividends. That deals with the waste and extravagance, and that may be the answer to the manager of the Weyburn Security Bank and to Sir John Aird and all the others who told us they could not carry on in western Canada if the rate of interest was reduced to 7 or 8 per cent. Their argument holds no water. No evidence has been adduced by them in support of it. We asked for someone to come before the committee and give evidence as to the average cost of managing a bank in western Canada, and we did not get them before that committee.
I have one last suggestion to make. If the hon. members of this House do not see fit to pass the amendment offered now by the hon. member for Macleod I would ask them to be logical and strike out something that is useless. If you will not pass the amendment to

this section, strike the section out. It is a camouflage, or worse, a futile falsehood. It does not guarantee anything to anybody, but the section is in the act in order to give confidence to the people. "There is a rate of interest fixed in Canada, and the banks cannot charge any more than the legal rate," is the false message conveyed. That is an utter farce, Mr. Chairman. Why perpetuate it? Cut it out, and let us be honest with ourselves and with the people who borrow money from the banks of Canada.

I had expected yesterday to
speak at considerable length on this question of the interest rate, but I do not want to speak to-night and I do not think anybody here wants me to speak. I would think the Minister of Finance would be courteous to the House if he would permit it to adjourn the debate until to-morrow. If not, it simply means that he is exercising the power which he has to suppress discussion.

Go on.

I do not propose, Mr. Chairman, to speak to-night under the circumstances. I simply give expression to this view that we ought after last night's experience to have a little chance of debating this matter to-morrow.
